metadata.title: VSEPR shapes: CF₂Cl₂, ICl₃, XeO₂F₄, SOF₄, IF₇
metadata.source: Tutorial 1 (RK1) Q A

variants.stem: Give the **molecular** geometry (VSEPR) of each species.
variants.hint: Count σ-bonds + lone pairs on the central atom (steric number), pick the electron-pair geometry, then name the shape from the atom positions only.
variants.explanation: Steric numbers: CF₂Cl₂ 4 (0 lp) → tetrahedral; ICl₃ 5 (2 lp, equatorial) → T-shaped; XeO₂F₄ 6 (0 lp; Xe=O counted as one domain) → octahedral; SOF₄ 5 (0 lp) → trigonal bipyramidal; IF₇ 7 → pentagonal bipyramidal. Electron-pair geometry key (Tutorial 1): tetrahedral, TBP, octahedral, TBP, pentagonal bipyramidal.

variants.stem: Which of CF₂Cl₂, ICl₃, XeO₂F₄ (O atoms trans), SOF₄ and IF₇ are **polar**? Select all.
variants.explanation: Polar: CF₂Cl₂ (C–F and C–Cl dipoles do not cancel), ICl₃ (T-shape), SOF₄ (S=O breaks the symmetry). Non-polar: trans-XeO₂F₄ and IF₇ (dipoles cancel by symmetry). Key: Tutorial 1 A.

metadata.title: Pick the polar molecule
metadata.source: Tutorial 1 (RK1) Q B

variants.stem: Choose the **polar** molecule.
variants.explanation: SO₂ is bent (steric number 3, one lone pair), so the S–O dipoles do not cancel. AlCl₃/SO₃ (trigonal planar), AlCl₄⁻/ClO₄⁻ (tetrahedral), BeCl₂/CO₂ (linear) and PF₅ (TBP) are all symmetric.

metadata.title: VSEPR shapes: SO₂, ICl₃, XeOF₄
metadata.source: Example test #1 (Prof Ito) Q2

variants.stem: Using VSEPR, give the molecular shape of each.
variants.explanation: SO₂: 2 bonding domains + 1 lone pair → bent. ICl₃: 3 bp + 2 lp (lone pairs equatorial) → T-shaped. XeOF₄: 5 bp + 1 lp → square pyramidal (O apical, lone pair trans to O).

metadata.title: VSEPR drill (hypervalent species)
metadata.source: Ch1 VSEPR slides (variants unverified)

variants.stem: Give the molecular shape of each species.
variants.explanation: SF₄: 4 bp + 1 lp (lp equatorial) → see-saw. XeF₄: 4 bp + 2 lp (lp trans) → square planar. I₃⁻: 2 bp + 3 lp (all equatorial) → linear.

variants.stem: Give the molecular shape of each species.
variants.explanation: ClF₃: 3 bp + 2 lp → T-shaped. BrF₅: 5 bp + 1 lp → square pyramidal. XeF₂: 2 bp + 3 lp → linear.

variants.stem: Solid PCl₅ is [PCl₄]⁺[PCl₆]⁻, and ICl₄⁻ is a classic hypervalent anion. Give the shape of each ion.
variants.explanation: [PCl₄]⁺: 4 bp → tetrahedral. [PCl₆]⁻: 6 bp → octahedral. [ICl₄]⁻: 4 bp + 2 lp → square planar. (Gas-phase PCl₅ itself is TBP.)

metadata.title: VSEPR repulsion hierarchy and bond angles
metadata.source: Ch1 VSEPR slides

variants.stem: Order the electron-pair repulsions.
variants.explanation: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp: lone pairs are held by one nucleus only, so they are more spread out and repel more. Repulsions at 90° matter most.

variants.stem: Order the bond angles.
variants.explanation: CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ 107.3° > H₂O 104.5°: each extra lone pair compresses the bond angles further.

metadata.title: Resonance structures of O₃, NO₃⁻, ClO₄⁻
metadata.source: Example test #1 Q1

variants.stem: How many equivalent resonance structures does each species have (the structures drawn in the course key)?
variants.explanation: O₃: the double bond can sit on either side (2). NO₃⁻: N=O can be on any of three O (3). ClO₄⁻ drawn with three Cl=O and one Cl–O⁻: the single-bonded O can be any of four (4). The course key marks a NO₃⁻ structure with an expanded octet on N as "not acceptable" because N (period 2) cannot exceed an octet.

variants.stem: Draw the Lewis structures (with resonance forms) of O₃, ClO₄⁻ and NO₃⁻.
variants.explanation: Course key (Example #1 Q1). Never give N, O or other period-2 atoms more than 8 electrons.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: O₃: two resonance forms, central O with one lone pair, formal charges +1 (central) and −1 (single-bonded O)
ClO₄⁻: Cl with three Cl=O and one Cl–O⁻ in each form (expanded octet), four equivalent forms
NO₃⁻: three forms, N with one N=O, no expanded octet on N, formal charge N +1

metadata.title: Formal charges in Al₂Cl₆ and I₂Cl₆
metadata.source: Tutorial 1 (RK1) Q C

variants.stem: Al₂Cl₆ and I₂Cl₆ both contain two bridging Cl atoms. Give the formal charge of each atom listed.
variants.explanation: FC = valence e − nonbonding e − bonds. Al: 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. I: 7 − 4 (two lone pairs) − 4 = −1. Bridging Cl: 7 − 4 − 2 = +1.

variants.stem: Al₂Cl₆ is non-planar but I₂Cl₆ is planar. Explain the structural difference.
variants.explanation: Key: only I₂Cl₆ is planar because each I has two lone pairs (octahedral electron-pair geometry), making each ICl₄ moiety square planar.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Al has no lone pairs: steric number 4 → each AlCl₄ unit is tetrahedral (non-planar dimer)
Each I carries two lone pairs: steric number 6 → octahedral electron-pair geometry
Lone pairs trans → each ICl₄ unit is square planar, so the whole I₂Cl₆ is planar

metadata.title: Why OF₄ does not exist but SF₄ does
metadata.source: Example test #2 Q10

variants.stem: SF₄ is a stable gas. Is the lighter analogue OF₄ likely to exist? Explain briefly.
variants.explanation: Key words: electron-pair geometry of OF₄ would be sp³d; because of the large energy gap, O d-orbitals cannot contribute to bonding.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: States OF₄ is not likely to exist
OF₄ would need an expanded valence shell (sp³d, 5 electron domains) around O
O (period 2) has no accessible d orbitals: energy gap too large, so it cannot exceed an octet

metadata.title: Octet-rule exceptions
metadata.source: Ch1 Lewis slides (exceptions #1, #2)

variants.stem: Select all species whose central atom has **fewer** than eight valence electrons (electron-deficient).
variants.explanation: Be tends to have 4 electrons and B 6 (electron-deficient, Lewis acidic). SF₆ and PCl₅ have expanded shells (period 3+); NH₃ and H₂O obey the octet.

variants.stem: Select all species that need an **expanded** valence shell on the central atom.
variants.explanation: Expanded shells start in period 3, where higher unoccupied orbitals become available: SF₆ (12 e), BrF₅ (12 e), XeF₄ (12 e).

metadata.title: Dative bond: NH₃ + BF₃
metadata.source: Ch1 Lewis slides (coordinate covalent bond)

variants.stem: NH₃ and BF₃ combine to form H₃N→BF₃.
variants.explanation: NH₃ donates its lone pair into the empty B 2p orbital (coordinate/dative bond). In the adduct N is +1 and B is −1; B changes from trigonal planar (sp²) to tetrahedral (sp³).

fields.label: Formal charge on B in the adduct

metadata.title: Counting ions in unit cells
metadata.source: Tutorial 1 (RK1) Q F

variants.stem: CsCl unit cell: Cs⁺ at the body centre, Cl⁻ at the 8 corners. Give the number of each ion per unit cell and the formula.
variants.explanation: Body centre counts 1; corners 8 × 1/8 = 1 → CsCl.

variants.stem: Rutile (TiO₂): Ti⁴⁺ at the 8 corners and the body centre; O²⁻ with 2 inside the cell and 4 on faces. Count the ions per unit cell.
variants.explanation: Ti: 1 (inside) + 8 × 1/8 = 2. O: 2 (inside) + 4 × 1/2 = 4. Ratio 2:4 → TiO₂.

variants.stem: Fluorite (CaF₂): Ca²⁺ at the 8 corners and 6 face centres; F⁻ in the 8 tetrahedral holes inside the cell. Count the ions per unit cell.
Perovskite: Ca²⁺ at the 8 corners, Ti⁴⁺ at the body centre, O²⁻ at the 6 face centres. Count the ions per unit cell.

metadata.title: Explaining boiling-point trends
metadata.source: Tutorial 1 (RK1) Q E

variants.stem: CH₃OH (bp 65 °C) boils far higher than CH₃Cl (bp −24 °C), although CH₃Cl is heavier. Explain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: CH₃OH molecules hydrogen-bond to each other (O–H···O); CH₃Cl cannot
C–Cl is less polar than C–O (Cl less electronegative)
Stronger intermolecular forces → more thermal energy needed to separate molecules

variants.stem: C₂H₅OH (78 °C) boils higher than CH₃OH (65 °C). Explain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Both are polar and H-bond in similar ways (one –OH each)
Ethanol is larger (more electrons, more polarisable) → stronger van der Waals/dispersion forces

variants.stem: HOCH₂CH₂OH (MW 62, bp 197 °C) boils much higher than isopropanol (MW 60, bp 82 °C). Explain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Similar molar mass, so dispersion forces are comparable
Ethylene glycol has two –OH groups → many more H-bonds per molecule

variants.stem: CH₃Cl (MW 50.5, bp −24 °C) boils higher than Cl₂ (MW 70, bp −34 °C). Explain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Cl₂ is non-polar: only dispersion forces
CH₃Cl is polar: dipole–dipole forces outweigh the heavier mass of Cl₂

metadata.title: Boiling/melting-point comparisons (quick picks)
metadata.source: Example tests #1 Q5–6, #2 Q1–2, #3 Q1, #X Q1, Q3

variants.stem: Which has the **highest** boiling point?
variants.explanation: Trisilane: largest, most polarisable molecule → strongest dispersion forces (Example #2 Q1).

variants.stem: Which has the **lowest** boiling point?
variants.explanation: NH₃ (−33 °C): N is the least electronegative and NH₃ has only one lone pair, so its H-bonding is weakest (Example #2 Q2, #3 Q1).

variants.stem: Which has the **highest** boiling point?
variants.explanation: Dispersion forces grow with chain length (Example #X Q1).

variants.stem: Which metal has the **highest** boiling point?
variants.explanation: More valence electrons per atom in the electron sea (1, 2, 3) → stronger metallic bonding (Example #X Q3).

variants.stem: The boiling point of H₂O is ___ that of NH₃.
variants.explanation: O is more electronegative and each H₂O can make two donor and two acceptor H-bonds (Example #1 Q5).

variants.stem: The melting point of Cs is ___ that of Rb.
variants.explanation: Metallic bonding weakens down Group 1 as atoms get larger (M–M bonding decreases Li → Cs) (Example #1 Q6).

metadata.title: Boiling points of H₂E (E = O, S, Se, Te)
metadata.source: Ch2 IMF slides (unverified variant)

variants.stem: Order by boiling point.
variants.explanation: H₂S (−60 °C) < H₂Se (−41 °C) < H₂Te (−2 °C) follow increasing dispersion; H₂O (100 °C) is anomalously high because of hydrogen bonding.

metadata.title: Ethane vs ammonia-borane
metadata.source: Example test #X Q11 → past finals P2 Q1(c) (verbatim, 5 marks)

variants.stem: Despite being isoelectronic and of similar molar mass, ethane (MW 30.07) is a gas (bp −89 °C) whereas ammonia-borane H₃N–BH₃ (MW 30.87) is a solid (mp 107 °C). Explain the difference in detail.
variants.explanation: Key idea: polarity + dihydrogen bonding (N–H···H–B) vs only London forces in ethane.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Ethane is non-polar: only weak dispersion forces
The dative N→B bond makes H₃N–BH₃ highly polar (N end δ+, B end δ−) → strong dipole–dipole forces
N–H hydrogens are protic (δ+) and B–H hydrogens are hydridic (δ−), because N is more and B less electronegative than H
N–Hδ+···δ−H–B dihydrogen bonds link neighbouring molecules into a solid

metadata.title: Why ice floats; volume change on freezing
metadata.source: Example test #2 Q11; Tutorial 2 (RK2) Q E

variants.stem: Briefly explain why ice floats on water.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: H₂O has tetrahedral electron-pair geometry (VSEPR)
Large O–H electronegativity difference → hydrogen bonding
In ice, H-bonding is maximised in an open, diamond-like lattice with empty space
Ice therefore has a larger volume / lower density than liquid water (maximum density at 4 °C)

variants.stem: At 283 K, 1 g of liquid water occupies 1 cm³; ice has density 0.92 g cm⁻³. By how much does the volume of 100 g of water **increase** on freezing?

inputSlot.formatHint: cm³, 1 decimal place

metadata.title: Heavy p-block elements: hybridization fails
metadata.source: Ch2 slides (double-bond rule, disilene); Tutorial 3 Q F; past finals P2 Q2(c)
metadata.memoryHook: **Heavier p-block atoms barely mix s and p**, so disilene is trans-bent and weakly bonded (donor–acceptor), unlike planar ethene. This is the double-bond rule.

variants.stem: Explain why CCl₄ is stable at room temperature, whereas PbCl₄ decomposes to PbCl₂ and Cl₂.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: For heavy elements the ns and np orbitals differ greatly in size and energy
So hybridization (promotion to form sp³) costs a large promotion energy
Total bond energy gained in PbCl₄ does not repay the promotion energy → Pb(IV) unstable, Pb(II) favoured (inert pair)

variants.stem: Acetylene HC≡CH is linear, but the heavier lead analogue RPbPbR is trans-bent with a bending angle near 90°. Explain.
variants.explanation: Same logic as the double-bond rule slide: disilene is trans-bent and weakly bonded (donor–acceptor), unlike planar ethene. The heavier the element, the less s–p mixing.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Large size and energy gap between 6s and 6p → Pb does not hybridize (6s stays as an inert lone pair)
Each RPb fragment uses essentially pure 6p orbitals for bonding (p orbitals are mutually at 90°)
Pb–Pb bonding is donor–acceptor: a lone pair on one Pb donates into an empty 6p orbital on the other (and vice versa)
Weak π overlap / Pauli repulsion means no true triple bond; result is a trans-bent, roughly 90° structure with a weak Pb–Pb bond

variants.stem: Which statements explain the weak, trans-bent Si=Si bond in disilenes? Select all.
variants.explanation: Double-bond rule (c. 1960): stable double bonds of period-3+ elements were thought impossible. Large ns/np size and energy gaps → poor hybridization, large promotion energy, Pauli repulsion → weak, reactive, trans-bent double bonds.

options.label: ns and np orbitals of Si differ greatly in size, so they hybridize poorly
Promotion energy to form hybrids is large
Si is more electronegative than C
The bond is better described by donor–acceptor interactions between two bent SiH₂ units

metadata.title: Classify solids by bonding type
metadata.source: Ch2 outline (molecular solids, covalent network, metals, ionic)

variants.stem: Classify each solid as **ionic**, **covalent network**, **molecular** or **metallic**.
variants.explanation: SiO₂: 3D lattice of Si–O single bonds. I₂ and dry ice: discrete molecules held by dispersion forces. Cu: metallic bonding. CsCl: ions.

metadata.title: Energetics of LiF formation
metadata.source: Ch3 textbook section 5.3.2 (LiF thermochemical steps)

variants.stem: Data (kJ mol⁻¹): sublimation of Li 161; IE(Li) 520; ½ D(F₂) 79; electron affinity of F, F(g) + e⁻ → F⁻(g), ΔH = −328; Li⁺(g) + F⁻(g) → LiF(s), ΔH = −1050.
variants.explanation: 161 + 520 + 79 − 328 = +432 kJ mol⁻¹ to make gas-phase ions; adding the lattice term −1050 gives −618 kJ mol⁻¹. Making the ions is strongly endothermic; the lattice enthalpy makes LiF formation spontaneous.

fields.label: ΔH for Li(s) + ½F₂(g) → Li⁺(g) + F⁻(g)

metadata.title: Shortest and longest bond: Li₂, C₂, F₂, N₂
metadata.source: Tutorial 2 (RK2) Q A

variants.stem: Among Li₂, C₂, F₂ and N₂, which has the shortest bond and which the longest? (MO theory)
variants.explanation: Bond orders: Li₂ 1, C₂ 2, N₂ 3, F₂ 1. N₂ has the highest bond order → shortest. Li₂ and F₂ both have bond order 1, but Li uses large 2s orbitals → longest (Li₂ 267 pm vs F₂ 141 pm).

metadata.title: Bond-order puzzle (X₂, Y₂, Z₂ from B, C, N, O)
metadata.source: Tutorial 2 (RK2) Q B

variants.stem: For p-block diatomics X₂, Y₂, Z₂ (X, Y, Z are three of B, C, N, O): bond order (X₂)⁺ = (Y₂)⁻ = (Z₂)⁻, and (X₂)⁻ = (Y₂)⁺ < Z₂. Identify X, Y and Z, and state which of the neutral X₂, Y₂, Z₂ move **out** of a magnetic field.
variants.explanation: Bond orders: O₂⁺ 2.5 = C₂⁻ 2.5 = N₂⁻ 2.5; O₂⁻ 1.5 = C₂⁺ 1.5 < N₂ 3. Moving out of the field = diamagnetic: C₂ (π_u⁴) and N₂. O₂ is paramagnetic.

metadata.title: Bond order and unpaired electrons of diatomics
metadata.source: Ch3 MO slides / textbook Fig. 5.7

variants.stem: Give the bond order (BO) and number of unpaired electrons (n) for each.
variants.explanation: B₂: π_u¹π_u¹ (s–p mixing puts σ_g(2p) above π_u) → BO 1, 2 unpaired. C₂: π_u⁴ → BO 2, diamagnetic. O₂: π_g*¹π_g*¹ → BO 2, 2 unpaired.

variants.stem: Give the O–O bond order of each dioxygen species.
variants.explanation: Removing a π* electron raises BO; adding π* electrons lowers it: O₂⁺ 2.5 (111.6 pm), O₂ 2 (120.8 pm), O₂⁻ 1.5 (135 pm, 1 unpaired), O₂²⁻ 1 (150 pm, diamagnetic).

variants.stem: Give the bond order of each species and the number of unpaired electrons in NO.
variants.explanation: NO has 11 valence electrons (one in π*): BO 2.5, paramagnetic. NO⁺ and CN⁻ are isoelectronic with N₂/CO (10 e) → BO 3. NO⁻ (12 e, like O₂) → BO 2 with two unpaired electrons.

metadata.title: O–O bond lengths in dioxygen species
metadata.source: Ch3 textbook Table 5.1

variants.stem: Order by O–O bond length.
variants.explanation: Bond order 1 < 1.5 < 2 < 2.5, so length O₂²⁻ (150 pm) > O₂⁻ (135) > O₂ (121) > O₂⁺ (112).

variants.stem: Order by N–O bond length.

metadata.title: s–p mixing and the magnetism of B₂ and C₂
metadata.source: Ch3 textbook 5.2.2–5.2.3

variants.stem: Explain, using s–p mixing, why B₂ is paramagnetic and C₂ diamagnetic, and why the effect disappears for O₂ and F₂.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: σ_g(2s) and σ_g(2p) have the same symmetry and similar energy, so they mix: σ_g(2s) is pushed down and σ_g(2p) pushed up
For B₂–N₂ the pushed-up σ_g(2p) lies above π_u(2p)
B₂: last two electrons go singly into the degenerate π_u pair (Hund) → paramagnetic; C₂: π_u⁴ with σ_g(2p) empty → diamagnetic
The 2s–2p gap grows with Z (5.7 eV for B to 21.5 eV for F), so mixing is weak for O₂/F₂ and the normal order (σ_g below π_u) returns

metadata.title: Electrons in the HOMO(s)
metadata.source: Example tests #2 Q5–6, #3 Q3, #X Q8 → past finals P3 Q1(d) (verbatim, 5 marks)

variants.stem: According to MO theory, what is the **total number of electrons** in the highest occupied molecular orbital(s) of methane, CH₄?
variants.explanation: CH₄ (T_d): a₁² t₂⁶. The HOMO is the triply degenerate t₂ set (C 2p + H group orbitals) holding 6 electrons — the 1:3 pattern seen in its photoelectron spectrum.

inputSlot.formatHint: Integer

variants.stem: Based on MO theory, how many electrons are in the HOMO of hydroxide, OH⁻? (H 1s lies higher in energy than O 2p.)
variants.explanation: Only O 2p_z overlaps H 1s (σ). O 2p_x and 2p_y are nonbonding and form the degenerate HOMO with 4 electrons (as in HF).

inputSlot.formatHint: Integer

variants.stem: Based on MO theory, how many electrons are in the HOMO of diatomic C₂?
variants.explanation: With s–p mixing, C₂ is (σ_g)²(σ_u*)²(π_u)⁴; the HOMO is the degenerate π_u pair with 4 electrons.

inputSlot.formatHint: Integer

metadata.title: HOMO electron counts (drill)
metadata.source: Ch3 MO diagrams (drill set, unverified variants)

variants.stem: Total number of electrons in the HOMO(s) of each (count all electrons in a degenerate HOMO set).
variants.explanation: N₂: σ_g(2p)² (above π_u by s–p mixing). O₂: π_g*¹π_g*¹ = 2. F₂: π_g*⁴. B₂: π_u¹π_u¹ = 2. CO: 3σ² (carbon lone pair).

variants.stem: Total number of electrons in the HOMO(s) of each.
variants.explanation: H₂O: 1b₂ (pure O 2p_y, nonbonding) 2 e. NH₃: 3a₁ (mostly N 2p_z, the lone pair) 2 e. HF: degenerate nonbonding F 2p_x/2p_y, 4 e. BH₃: degenerate e′ bonding pair, 4 e (LUMO is the empty B 2p_z, a₂″).

metadata.title: MO diagram of NF
metadata.source: Example test #1 Q3

variants.stem: NF is made by photolysis of FN₃ in an argon matrix at 4 K. Give its bond order and magnetism.
variants.explanation: NF has 12 valence electrons (isoelectronic with O₂): ...(π)⁴(π*)¹(π*)¹ → BO 2 and two unpaired electrons → paramagnetic.

variants.stem: Construct the MO diagram of NF and fill the electrons (no symmetry labels needed).

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: F atomic orbitals drawn lower than N (F more electronegative)
σ(2s), σ*(2s), σ(2p), π(2p)×2, π*×2, σ* in a sensible order with lines to parent AOs
12 valence electrons placed; last two singly in the two π* orbitals (Hund)
Bonding MOs drawn closer to F, antibonding closer to N

metadata.title: Nitrene (NH): MO diagram and spin multiplicity
metadata.source: Past finals P2 Q2(a) (6 marks)

variants.stem: Nitrene NH is a heteronuclear diatomic. H 1s lies only slightly higher than N 2p. Using MO theory, give:
variants.explanation: 6 valence electrons. N 2s is too low to mix much (≈ nonbonding, 2 e). H 1s + N 2p_z → σ (2 e) and σ*. N 2p_x, 2p_y are nonbonding and degenerate: the last 2 electrons occupy them singly → S = 1, triplet (multiplicity 3).

variants.stem: Draw the MO diagram of nitrene (NH) and disclose its spin multiplicity.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: N 2s low and essentially nonbonding (filled)
Only N 2p_z combines with H 1s: one σ bonding (filled) and one σ* (empty)
N 2p_x and 2p_y nonbonding, degenerate, each holding one electron with parallel spins
States triplet (2S+1 = 3)

metadata.title: Three-centre π systems: allyl and ozone
metadata.source: Tutorial 3 Q A; past finals P1 Q2(d) (ozone, 10 marks)

variants.stem: For the π system of the allyl cation C₃H₅⁺:
variants.explanation: π₁ (0 nodes, bonding) holds both electrons; π₂ (node through central C) is nonbonding; π₃ antibonding. π bond order per C–C = ½ (one π bond over two links), so each C–C = 1 (σ) + ½ (π) = 1.5.

fields.label: HOMO (π₁ bonding / π₂ nonbonding / π₃ antibonding)
Total bond order of each C–C (σ + π)

variants.stem: Ozone O₃ is bent with an sp² central O. For its π-type molecular orbitals (π₁ bonding, π₂ nonbonding, π₃ antibonding), give the electron count in each and the total bond order of each O–O bond.
variants.explanation: Ozone has 4 π electrons (isoelectronic π system with the allyl anion): π₁² π₂² π₃⁰. Only π₁ is bonding → π bond order ½ per O–O; with the σ bond each O–O = 1.5, consistent with two equivalent resonance structures.

variants.stem: Draw the π-type MOs of ozone (O₃), give the electron configuration of the π system and the bond order of each O–O bond (consider σ and π).

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Three p_π orbitals (one per O) combine into three MOs
π₁: all in phase, no node, bonding
π₂: node through the central O, terminal p orbitals out of phase, nonbonding
π₃: two nodes, antibonding
4 π electrons: π₁² π₂²
Bond order per O–O = 1 (σ) + 0.5 (π) = 1.5

metadata.title: Triatomic hydrogen cation H₃⁺
metadata.source: Tutorial 3 Q B; textbook Exercise 5.4

variants.stem: For **cyclic** H₃⁺ (equilateral triangle), what is the bond order of each H–H link?
variants.explanation: Three 1s orbitals → one a₁′ bonding MO and a degenerate e′ antibonding pair. The 2 electrons fill a₁′: total BO = 1 shared over 3 links → 1/3 each.

inputSlot.formatHint: Fraction or decimal

variants.stem: For **linear** H–H–H⁺, what is the bond order of each H–H link?
variants.explanation: Linear: σ_g bonding, nonbonding, σ_u* antibonding. 2 electrons in the bonding MO → BO 1 over two links = ½ each (a 3-centre 2-electron bond).

inputSlot.formatHint: Fraction or decimal

metadata.title: MO description of BH₃ and its Lewis acidity
metadata.source: Tutorial 3 Q C

variants.stem: From the MO diagram of trigonal planar BH₃:
variants.explanation: Six valence electrons fill a₁′ and e′ bonding MOs (three B–H bonds, BO 1 each). The B 2p_z (a₂″) has no matching H group orbital and is empty: it is the LUMO that accepts an electron pair.

fields.label: Number of valence electrons in the MOs

metadata.title: Ligand group orbitals of six H atoms in O_h
metadata.source: Tutorial 3 Q D; Ch7 LFT slides (octahedral LGOs) — drafted from course notes (unverified)

variants.stem: Six H 1s orbitals in an octahedron form six LGOs. Give the symmetry labels and which is lowest in energy.
variants.explanation: Γ(6 H 1s) = a₁g + t₁u + e_g. The a₁g LGO (all in phase, no nodes) is lowest; t₁u (one node) and e_g (two nodes) are higher. The same pattern gives the σ framework of every octahedral complex.

fields.label: How many LGOs of t₁u symmetry?

variants.stem: Draw the six σ-type ligand group orbitals of an octahedral ML₆ complex (each ligand contributes one σ orbital pointing at M), as shown in the lectures. Show the signs of the lobes, group them by symmetry label, and say which metal orbital each group can overlap with.
variants.explanation: The six σ LGOs split into a₁g + t₁u + e_g. a₁g (no nodes) is lowest; t₁u has one node and e_g two. Each LGO overlaps only with the metal orbitals of matching symmetry; t₂g has none, which is why the t₂g set stays non-bonding (and defines the d-orbital splitting in LFT).

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: a₁g: one LGO with all six ligand orbitals in phase; it matches the metal s orbital
t₁u: three LGOs, each built from the pair of ligands on one axis with opposite signs (x, y, z); they match the metal p_x, p_y, p_z
e_g: two LGOs — one with the z-axis pair in phase and the four equatorial ligands out of phase, and one with the x pair in phase and the y pair out of phase; they match the metal d_z² and d_x²−y²
The metal d_xy, d_xz, d_yz (t₂g) point between the ligands and have no σ LGO partner, so they are non-bonding in a σ-only complex

variants.stem: Which statement correctly matches the σ LGOs of an octahedral complex to the metal orbitals?
variants.explanation: Overlap requires matching symmetry (the labels tell you which orbitals can interact). a₁g has the symmetry of s, t₁u of p, e_g of d_z² and d_x²−y²; d_xy, d_xz and d_yz (t₂g) have no matching LGO in a σ-only complex.

options.label: a₁g ↔ s; t₁u ↔ p_x, p_y, p_z; e_g ↔ d_z² and d_x²−y²; d_xy, d_xz, d_yz are non-bonding
a₁g ↔ s; t₁u ↔ p_x, p_y, p_z; e_g ↔ all five d orbitals
a₁g ↔ p; t₁u ↔ s; e_g ↔ d_xy, d_xz, d_yz
Every LGO overlaps with the metal d_xy, d_xz, d_yz

metadata.title: Three-centre four-electron hydrogen bonds
metadata.source: Example test #X Q12; past finals P1 Q2(a) (Zundel, 5 marks)

variants.stem: In symmetric [F–H–F]⁻, considering the σ system built from F 2p_z group orbitals and H 1s:
variants.explanation: Three orbitals → bonding (2 e), nonbonding (2 e, on the F atoms), antibonding (empty). One bonding pair over two links → BO 0.5 each: a 3c-4e bond.

fields.label: Bond order of each H–F link

variants.stem: The F···H interaction in [F–H–F]⁻ (39.4 kcal mol⁻¹) is much stronger than the hydrogen bond between HF molecules (6.9 kcal mol⁻¹). Explain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Symmetric F–H–F is a 3-centre-4-electron (3c-4e) bond
MO: bonding (filled), nonbonding (filled, on F), antibonding (empty)
Each F–H link has bond order 0.5, far more than an ordinary electrostatic H-bond

variants.stem: The Zundel cation [H₅O₂]⁺ contains a symmetric O···H···O hydrogen bond (138 kJ mol⁻¹). Using MO theory, explain in detail why it is much stronger than the asymmetric O–H···O hydrogen bond between water molecules (20 kJ mol⁻¹).

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Ordinary O–H···O hydrogen bond is a weak, mainly electrostatic interaction (δ+ H with an O lone pair)
In the symmetric case the two O donor orbitals form in-phase and out-of-phase group orbitals; only the in-phase one matches H 1s
Result: bonding MO (2 e), nonbonding MO (2 e, on the O atoms), antibonding MO (empty) → 3c-4e bond
Bond order 0.5 for each O–H, i.e. genuinely covalent, hence much stronger

metadata.title: Electron-deficient multicentre bonds
metadata.source: Example tests #3 Q8, #X Q7; Ch4 diborane / MeLi / BeMe₂ slides

variants.stem: The MeLi tetramer involves ___ bonds.
variants.explanation: Each CH₃ caps a Li₃ face of the Li₄ tetrahedron: one carbon orbital + three Li orbitals share 2 electrons (4c-2e). (Example #3 Q8.)

variants.stem: The bridging Be–CH₃–Be bonds in polymeric dimethylberyllium are ___ bonds.
variants.explanation: Each bridging C uses one orbital shared with two Be orbitals by 2 electrons (3c-2e). C looks 5-coordinate but is not dsp³: coordination number does not fix hybridization. (Example #X Q7.)

variants.stem: For diborane B₂H₆:
variants.explanation: Each bridge: one sp³ orbital from each B + H 1s → bonding (2 e), nonbonding, antibonding MOs. Two bridges, each a 3c-2e bond with B–H bond order 0.5; four ordinary terminal B–H bonds. (AlH₃)ₙ similarly has six Al–H–Al 3c-2e interactions per octahedral Al.

fields.label: Bond order of each bridging B–H

metadata.title: Why CO binds to metals through carbon
metadata.source: Ch3 textbook 5.3.1 (CO frontier orbitals)

variants.stem: Electronegativity would suggest CO binds metals through O, yet nearly all carbonyls are M–C–O. Use the MO diagram of CO to explain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: The HOMO (3σ) has its largest lobe on C (C 2s and 2p_z both mix with O 2p_z) → the donated lone pair is carbon-based
The LUMOs (π*) are also concentrated on C, so π back-donation from the metal is best through C

variants.stem: Which conditions are needed for two atomic orbitals to form bonding/antibonding MOs? Select all.
variants.explanation: Symmetry, energy match and distance. AOs more than about 10–14 eV apart barely interact.

options.label: Short enough distance for good overlap

variants.stem: In a heteronuclear diatomic AB (B more electronegative), which statements are true? Select all.
variants.explanation: The AO closer in energy to an MO contributes more to it: bonding MOs resemble the lower (B) orbitals, antibonding MOs the higher (A) orbitals.

options.label: B atomic orbitals lie lower in energy
Bonding MOs have more B character
Antibonding MOs have more A character
Bonding MOs have more A character

variants.stem: In a photoelectron spectrum, an ionisation band with extensive vibrational fine structure indicates removal of an electron from a…
variants.explanation: Removing a bonding electron changes the bond strongly, exciting many vibrational levels (e.g. π_u bands of N₂ and O₂).

metadata.title: Lone pairs in the MO pictures of H₂O and NH₃
metadata.source: Ch3 textbook 5.4.3–5.4.4

variants.stem: Which statements about the MO description of H₂O are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: Occupied: 2a₁ (mostly O 2s), 1b₁ and 3a₁ (bonding), 1b₂ (nonbonding O 2p_y). O 2s is ~19 eV below H 1s, so it barely interacts.

options.label: The HOMO (1b₂) is a pure O 2p orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane, nonbonding
The two "lone pairs" are not equivalent
The H group orbitals have A₁ and B₁ symmetry
All four occupied MOs are degenerate
O 2s interacts strongly with the H 1s orbitals

variants.stem: The HOMO of NH₃ is best described as…
variants.explanation: H group orbitals: A₁ + E. N 2s and 2p_z (A₁) combine with the A₁ group orbital; the HOMO (3a₁) is mostly N 2p_z with weak overlap with the H₃ triangle.

options.label: a slightly bonding a₁ orbital, mostly N 2p_z — the lone pair donated as a Lewis base
a degenerate e pair of N–H bonding orbitals

variants.stem: Which statements about the MO picture of BF₃ are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: σ: a₁′ + e′. π: a₂″ bonding (weak, B and F 2p differ by >10 eV) and a₂″ π* LUMO, mostly B 2p_z — the electron-pair acceptor.

options.label: The LUMO is a π* (a₂″) orbital with large empty lobes on B
A filled a₂″ π orbital delocalised over all four atoms gives slight B–F double-bond character
The σ framework uses B 2s, 2p_x, 2p_y (a₁′ + e′)

metadata.title: Group orbitals of CO₂ (qualitative)
metadata.source: Ch3 textbook 5.4.2 (qualitative use only); LGO slides — drafted from course notes (unverified)

variants.stem: CO₂ is linear (z along O–C–O). Draw the group orbitals formed from the two O 2p_z orbitals and from the two O 2p_x orbitals (in-phase and out-of-phase combinations), and show which carbon orbital, if any, each can overlap with.
variants.explanation: Group orbitals are sums and differences of the equivalent O orbitals. Only those with the same symmetry as a carbon valence orbital interact (C 2s, 2p_z → σ; C 2p_x, 2p_y → π). The remaining π combinations have no carbon partner and stay non-bonding on O.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: O 2p_z group orbitals: the combination symmetric about the carbon (g) matches C 2s; the antisymmetric combination (u) matches C 2p_z (both give σ interactions)
O 2p_x group orbitals: the combination with the same sign on both oxygens (u) matches C 2p_x (π interaction); likewise 2p_y
The other combination of O 2p_x (and 2p_y), with opposite signs on the two oxygens (g), has no matching carbon valence orbital, so it is non-bonding
Overlap is limited to orbitals of matching symmetry; C 2s is closer in energy to the O 2p_z group orbital than to O 2s

variants.stem: In CO₂, why do some of the O 2p group orbitals remain non-bonding?
variants.explanation: Overlap requires matching symmetry. The out-of-phase (g) combinations of the O 2p_x and 2p_y orbitals have no carbon 2p partner and (without carbon d orbitals) cannot interact, so they remain non-bonding oxygen lone-pair-like orbitals.

options.label: They have no carbon valence orbital of matching symmetry to overlap with
They are too high in energy
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it cannot form π bonds

metadata.title: Ionisation energy of PhSiMe₃ vs toluene
metadata.source: Past finals P1 Q2(c) (5 marks); Ch4 silyl-group slides

variants.stem: Explain in detail why the first ionisation energy of (trimethylsilyl)benzene C₆H₅SiMe₃ (9.05 eV) is greater than that of toluene C₆H₅CH₃ (8.84 eV).

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: The first IE removes an electron from the aromatic π HOMO
In toluene, filled C–H σ orbitals of CH₃ donate into the ring π system (hyperconjugation) → HOMO destabilised (raised) → lower IE
In PhSiMe₃, the low-lying σ*(Si–C) orbitals accept π density (negative hyperconjugation) → HOMO stabilised (lowered) → higher IE
Notes that this π-acceptor effect outweighs the simple inductive expectation from electropositive Si (EN Si 1.7 vs C 2.5)

metadata.title: (Valency, oxidation number, formal charge, coordination number)
metadata.source: Tutorial 2 (RK2) Q C(i); Example tests #3 Q4, #X Q9

variants.stem: For the **O** atom in the oxonium ion [OH₃]⁺, give the four quantities (course definitions).
variants.explanation: Course key: (4, −2, +1, 3). Valency here = valence electrons of the neutral atom minus lone-pair electrons (6 − 2 = 4); ON: each H +1 → O −2; FC = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; three attached atoms → CN 3.

variants.stem: For the **B** atom in [BH₄]⁻, give the four quantities (course definitions).
variants.explanation: Course key (h): (3, +3, −1, 4). H (χ 2.2) is more electronegative than B (2.0), so H is −1 and B +3; FC = 3 − 0 − 4 = −1; CN 4.

metadata.title: Assign oxidation numbers
metadata.source: Tutorial 2 (RK2) Q C(ii)
metadata.memoryHook: **H is −1 when bonded to a metal (hydride), +1 with nonmetals**: KH (−1); [ReH₉]²⁻ makes Re +7; H₃PO₂ makes P +1.

variants.stem: Give the oxidation number of the indicated atom.
variants.explanation: H is +1 with non-metals but −1 in metal hydrides (KH, [ReH₉]²⁻: Re + 9(−1) = −2 → Re +7). H₂PO(OH) = H₃PO₂ (phosphinic acid): 3(+1) + P + 2(−2) = 0 → P +1.

metadata.title: Average oxidation numbers: Mn₃O₄ and Mg₅Ga₂
metadata.source: Past finals P3 Q1(c) (verbatim, 5 marks)
metadata.memoryHook: **An average oxidation number can hide different atoms**: Mn₃O₄ is +8/3 on average, really Mn(II) + 2 Mn(III). The electropositive partner takes its usual charge: Mg is +2, so Ga is −5 in Mg₅Ga₂.

variants.stem: Give the **average** oxidation number of (i) Mn in manganese oxide Mn₃O₄ and (ii) Ga in pentamagnesium digallide Mg₅Ga₂.
variants.explanation: Mn₃O₄: 3x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +8/3 (it is Mn(II)Mn(III)₂O₄). Mg₅Ga₂: Mg is the electropositive partner, +2 each: 5(+2) + 2x = 0 → x = −5.

metadata.title: Oxidation numbers of N in its oxides
metadata.source: Tutorial 3 Q G; Example tests #2 Q8, #3 Q6
metadata.memoryHook: **The N oxides climb by +1**: N₂O (+1), NO (+2), N₂O₃ (+3), NO₂ (+4), N₂O₅ (+5). O is always −2, so count N.

variants.stem: Give the (average) oxidation number of N.
variants.explanation: Each O is −2: N₂O +1, NO +2, N₂O₃ +3 (the structure in Example #2 Q8/#3 Q6), NO₂ +4, N₂O₅ +5. In N₂O the two N atoms are not equivalent, but their average is +1.

metadata.title: Oxidation state of P in phosphorous acid
metadata.source: Past finals P1 Q1(a) (5 marks); Example test #3 Q11
metadata.memoryHook: **Phosphor-OUS is the lower state (+3), phosphor-IC the higher (+5).** PCl₃ + 3H₂O → H₃PO₃ + 3HCl; one H is on P and does not ionise, so it is diprotic.

variants.stem: Phosphorous acid is obtained when PCl₃ is treated with water. What is the oxidation state of P in phosphorous acid?
variants.explanation: PCl₃ + 3H₂O → H₃PO₃ + 3HCl. H₃PO₃ = HP(O)(OH)₂ (one P–H, two P–OH): 3(+1) + P + 3(−2) = 0 → P +3. Only the two O–H hydrogens are acidic (diprotic).

inputSlot.formatHint: Signed integer

variants.stem: Draw the structures of (a) phosphonic acid (P(+III)) and (b) phosphinic acid (P(+I)).
variants.explanation: Example #3 Q11. Count P–H bonds: each P–H instead of P–OH lowers the P oxidation state by 2 and removes one acidic proton.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Phosphonic acid: tetrahedral P with one P=O, one P–H and two P–OH (HP(O)(OH)₂)
Phosphinic acid: tetrahedral P with one P=O, two P–H and one P–OH (H₂P(O)OH)

metadata.title: Chlorine dioxide from sodium chlorate

metadata.title: Classes of hydrides
metadata.source: Example test #1 Q8; Ch4 Hydrogen slides
metadata.memoryHook: **Salt-like hydrides belong to the “salty” s-block**: only Li–Cs and Ca–Ba are electropositive enough to hand H an electron (H⁻). BeH₂ is covalent and polymeric; TiH₁.₈ is metallic and non-stoichiometric.

variants.stem: Which are **saline (ionic) hydrides**? Select all.

metadata.title: Why D₂ has a stronger bond than H₂
metadata.source: Example test #2 Q3 → past finals P2 Q2(b) (6 marks)
metadata.memoryHook: **Heavier isotope → lower zero-point energy → sits deeper in the well → stronger bond.** D₂ 106.0 vs H₂ 104.2 kcal/mol: the heavy one sits still, so more energy is needed to pull it apart.

variants.stem: The bond enthalpy of D–D is ___ that of H–H.
variants.explanation: D₂ 106.0 vs H₂ 104.2 kcal mol⁻¹ (Example #2 Q3).

variants.stem: Explain in detail why the bond enthalpy of H₂ (104.2 kcal mol⁻¹) is smaller than that of D₂ (106.0 kcal mol⁻¹).
variants.explanation: B = −(E_electronic + E₀) with E_electronic < 0, E₀ > 0. Heavier isotope → smaller E₀ → larger B. Hydrogen isotopes have the largest relative mass difference of any element, so the effect is largest here.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Same electronic potential-energy curve / same force constant f for H–H and D–D (isotopes are chemically identical)
Reduced mass μ(D₂) = 2 μ(H₂)
Vibrational frequency ω ∝ (f/μ)^½ is lower for D₂
Zero-point energy E₀ = ½hω (∝ (f/μ)^½) is lower for D₂, so D₂ sits deeper in the well
Bond enthalpy = depth of well − E₀, so a smaller E₀ gives a larger bond enthalpy for D₂

metadata.title: Kinetic isotope effect: CH₄ vs CD₄ chlorination
metadata.source: Past finals P3 Q2(d) (5 marks)
metadata.memoryHook: **C–H breaks faster than C–D.** C–D starts lower (lower zero-point energy), so it has further to climb to the transition state: CH₄ chlorinates faster than CD₄. “D is lazy: it sits low, so it climbs slowly.”

variants.stem: Photochemically initiated chlorination of CH₄ is faster than that of CD₄. Explain in detail.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Rate-determining step involves breaking C–H (C–D) by H(D) abstraction: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•
Greater reduced mass for C–D → lower vibrational frequency → lower zero-point energy
C–D therefore sits lower in the well; transition state has similar energy for both (bond largely broken)
Activation energy is larger for C–D → slower reaction (primary kinetic isotope effect)

metadata.title: Hydrogen storage capacity of NaAlH₄
metadata.source: Tutorial 2 (RK2) Q F
metadata.memoryHook: **Weight % H = (mass of H released) ÷ (mass of compound) × 100.** The usable figure is lower than the theoretical 7.47% because not all the H comes out: 3 mol NaAlH₄ give 4.5 mol H₂, which is 5.60%.

variants.stem: NaAlH₄ (M = 54.00 g mol⁻¹) decomposes: (1) 3NaAlH₄ → Na₃AlH₆ + 2Al + 3H₂; (2) Na₃AlH₆ → 3NaH + Al + 1.5H₂; (3) 3NaH → 3Na + 1.5H₂ (only above 670 K). H = 1.008.

metadata.title: Activating H₂: surfaces and metal complexes
metadata.source: Ch4 Hydrogen slides (1-2, 1-3: Kubas and Vaska complexes)
metadata.memoryHook: **Vaska’s complex, IrCl(CO)(PPh₃)₂ (Vaska and DiLuzio, 1961), is the textbook oxidative addition: Ir(I) → Ir(III), coordination number +2.** Kubas (1984) showed H₂ can also bind intact and side-on, not only as two hydrides: the intermediate on the way.
metadata.memoryHookNote: Who first made Vaska’s complex is contested (a crystallographic review credits an earlier preparation to Angoletta), so the credit here is for the 1961 formulation, not for priority.

variants.stem: Which statements are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: Oxidative addition raises the oxidation state by 2 (Ir(I) → Ir(III)) and the coordination number by 2. Dihydrogen and metal-hydride complexes are intermediates in catalytic hydrogenation.

options.label: Kubas complex W(η²-H₂)(CO)₃(PⁱPr₃)₂ keeps the H–H bond, binding H₂ side-on as a ligand
Vaska's complex cleaves H₂ by oxidative addition at Ir, square planar → octahedral
Oxidative addition of H₂ lowers the metal oxidation state by 2
H₂ cleavage on Pt is favourable because two Pt–H bonds (>70 kcal mol⁻¹ each) outweigh H–H (104 kcal mol⁻¹)

variants.stem: Why is H(g) → H⁺(g) + e⁻ so much more endothermic (313.6 kcal mol⁻¹) than for Li (122.7 kcal mol⁻¹)?
variants.explanation: 1s is much lower in energy than ns of the alkali metals and is unshielded, so H behaves more like a non-metal (its IE, EA, EN and bond energies resemble Group 14).

options.label: The H 1s electron has no inner-shell shielding and sits close to the nucleus
H has a half-filled p subshell
H⁺ is strongly hydrated in the gas phase

metadata.title: Radical-chain formation of HCl
metadata.source: Ch4 Hydrogen slides (reactivity of H₂, Ex 2)
metadata.memoryHook: **Start, carry on, stop**: light splits the weak Cl–Cl bond (243 kJ/mol); Cl• takes H from H₂; H• takes Cl from Cl₂ and gives Cl• back, so the chain feeds itself until radicals recombine.

variants.stem: Put the steps of the light-initiated H₂ + Cl₂ chain in mechanistic order (initiation, propagation, propagation, termination).
variants.explanation: Photolysis of the weak Cl–Cl bond (243 kJ mol⁻¹) initiates; Cl• abstracts H from H₂; H• abstracts Cl from Cl₂ regenerating Cl•; radical recombination terminates.

metadata.title: Alkali metals + O₂: oxide, peroxide, superoxide
metadata.source: Example test #1 Q7(a); past finals P1 Q1(b), P2 Q1(a)
metadata.memoryHook: **Bigger cation, bigger anion**: Li⁺ takes O²⁻ (oxide), Na⁺ takes O₂²⁻ (peroxide), K⁺ and heavier take O₂⁻ (superoxide). Lattice energy is best when the ion sizes match.

variants.stem: Give the principal product when each metal burns in O₂ (no water present).
variants.explanation: 4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O (oxide, O²⁻); 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂ (peroxide, O₂²⁻); K + O₂ → KO₂ (superoxide, O₂⁻; also Rb, Cs). Larger cations stabilise larger anions.

variants.stem: Disclose the principal product from the reaction of potassium with oxygen in the absence of water.
variants.explanation: K + O₂ → KO₂, containing the paramagnetic superoxide ion O₂⁻ (bond order 1.5, one unpaired electron).

inputSlot.formatHint: Formula or name

variants.stem: Disclose the **spin multiplicity** of the metal oxide obtained from sodium and oxygen.
variants.explanation: 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂. The peroxide ion O₂²⁻ has π*⁴ (bond order 1): all electrons paired, S = 0 → singlet, multiplicity 1 (diamagnetic). Compare KO₂: O₂⁻ is a doublet (2).

inputSlot.formatHint: 2S+1 value or name (e.g. 1 / singlet)

variants.stem: Write the reaction of sodium peroxide with water.
variants.explanation: Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂O₂ (peroxide ion is protonated to H₂O₂).

metadata.title: Hydration energy and charge density
metadata.source: Example test #X Q4 → past finals P3 Q1(b) (5 marks)
metadata.memoryHook: **Charge density = charge ÷ radius.** The more concentrated the charge, the more water it grabs: Al³⁺ (high charge, small) beats everything; within a group, Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺.

variants.stem: Among Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺, F⁻, Cl⁻, which ion has the **largest** hydration energy?
variants.explanation: Hydration energy scales with charge density (charge/radius): Al³⁺ has the highest charge and smallest radius.

variants.stem: Which ion has the largest hydration energy?
variants.explanation: Li⁺ is smallest → strongest ion–dipole interaction.

variants.stem: Order the Group 1 cations by magnitude of hydration enthalpy.
variants.explanation: Li⁺ 519 > Na⁺ 406 > K⁺ 322 > Rb⁺ 293 > Cs⁺ 264 kJ mol⁻¹ — decreasing as ionic radius grows (0.9 → 1.8 Å).

metadata.title: HSAB, lattice energy and solubility
metadata.source: Example test #X Q6; Tutorial 2 additional Q; Ch4 Group 1 solubility slides

variants.stem: In general, the solubility of LiF is ___ that of LiClO₄.
variants.explanation: LiF: hard–hard, best size match → very large lattice energy → sparingly soluble. LiClO₄: mismatched sizes → small lattice energy, and the high solvation energy of Li⁺ wins → very soluble (59.8 g/100 mL).

variants.stem: Solid CsCl, but not LiCl, absorbs HCl at low temperature (MCl + HCl ⇌ M[HCl₂]). Suggest an explanation.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Equilibrium position is governed by the relative lattice energies of MCl and M[HCl₂]
Cl⁻ is a hard base; Li⁺ is a hard acid, Cs⁺ a soft acid (HSAB)
LiCl (hard–hard, small ions) has a much larger lattice energy, so it is more stable and does not react; CsCl gains by forming the salt of the large [HCl₂]⁻ anion

metadata.title: Crown ethers and cryptands
metadata.source: Example tests #1 Q9, #2 Q9, #3 Q5; past finals P1 Q1(e); Ch4 Group 1 complex-ion slides
metadata.memoryHook: **Pedersen (1967) named crown ethers for their crown-shaped models; Lehn with Dietrich and Sauvage (1969) added the 3D cage, the cryptand, which holds ions tighter.** Fit by size: Li⁺ 1.36, Na⁺ 1.9, K⁺ 2.66, Cs⁺ 3.38 Å. Pedersen and Lehn shared the 1987 Nobel with Cram.

variants.stem: Which alkali-metal ion best fits each crown ether cavity?
Order the affinity of 18-crown-6 for the alkali-metal ions (treat Na⁺ and Cs⁺ as roughly equal; put Cs⁺ before Na⁺).
variants.explanation: Example #1 Q9 key: K⁺ > Rb⁺ > Cs⁺ ~ Na⁺ > Li⁺. Affinity peaks where ion size matches the cavity; binding is largely electrostatic.

variants.stem: Draw 18-crown-6 and briefly explain its affinity for alkali-metal ions.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: 18-membered ring: six O atoms separated by –CH₂CH₂– units (12 C, 6 O)
Binding is electrostatic: O lone pairs point into the cavity (hard O donors for hard M⁺)
Affinity depends on matching cavity size and ion size: best for K⁺

variants.stem: Clearly draw the Lewis structure of 2.2.1-cryptand (past finals P1 Q1(e)).
variants.explanation: Cryptands [2.2.2], [2.2.1], [2.1.1] differ in O count per bridge. Being bicyclic with N and O donors, they wrap the cation completely and bind more strongly and selectively than crowns.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Two bridgehead N atoms (tertiary amines), each with a lone pair pointing into the cavity
Three bridges linking the two N atoms; the numbers 2, 2, 1 = number of ether O atoms in each bridge
Two bridges –CH₂CH₂OCH₂CH₂OCH₂CH₂– and one bridge –CH₂CH₂OCH₂CH₂–
Overall C₁₈H₃₆N₂O₅ (5 O, 2 N donors), bicyclic

metadata.title: Electrides and alkalides
metadata.source: Ch4 Group 1 slides (electrides, alkalides)
metadata.memoryHook: **Dye’s group made the first crystalline alkalides (alkali metal as the anion) and electrides (the electron is the anion).** Alkalides form by 2Na → Na⁺ + Na⁻, driven by a crown or cryptand wrapping the Na⁺. Both are very strong reducing agents.

variants.stem: Which statements are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: Alkalides form by disproportionation 2Na → Na⁺ + Na⁻, driven by complexation of M⁺ (crown/cryptand). M⁻ species are very strong reducing agents (not oxidising) and need inert conditions. Li is the exception that does not form M⁻.

options.label: Dilute solutions of alkali metals in liquid NH₃ are blue and contain solvated electrons
In [Na(crypt-222)]⁺Na⁻, sodium is present in oxidation states +1 and −1

metadata.title: Group 2 oxides, carbonates and hydroxides

metadata.title: Anomalous beryllium and diagonal relationships
metadata.source: Ch4 Group 2 slides (anomalous Be, hydroxides, halides, diagonal relationships)
metadata.memoryHook: **Be bites both ways (diagonal to Al)**: Be(OH)₂ dissolves in acid *and* in base to give [Be(OH)₄]²⁻, just like Al(OH)₃. It is amphoteric.

variants.stem: Be(OH)₂ is amphoteric. Write its reaction with NaOH.
variants.explanation: Be(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂[Be(OH)₄]; it also dissolves in acid: Be(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → BeSO₄ + 2H₂O.

inputSlot.formatHint: Integer coefficients · one equation per line · charges with ^ (e.g. NH4^+, [AlH4]^-)

variants.stem: Give the diagonal partner (period 3, one group to the right) of each element.
variants.explanation: Similar charge density / electronegativity: Li–Mg (nitrides, carbonates that decompose on heating, covalent organometallics), Be–Al (amphoteric oxides/hydroxides, covalent halides), B–Si (hydridic hydrides).

variants.stem: Why do beryllium compounds generally show greater covalent character than the corresponding compounds of the heavier Group 2 metals? Select all that apply.
variants.explanation: Both keys come from Be being small: its Be²⁺ ion is highly polarising (strong distortion of the anion, so electron sharing), and the same small size makes Be the most electronegative Group 2 element, so the electronegativity difference with a given anion is smaller. They are two views of one cause, not two independent reasons. Be has no occupied d orbitals and the smallest, not the largest, atomic radius in Group 2. BeCl₂ forms chains (solid) and is a strong Lewis acid; BeF₂ is the most ionic Be compound yet has a low mp and low conductivity.

options.label: Be²⁺ is very small with a high charge density, so it strongly distorts the electron clouds of neighbouring anions and increases electron sharing
Be is more electronegative than the heavier Group 2 metals, so its electronegativity difference with a given anion is smaller and the bond is less ionic
Be has filled d orbitals that allow it to form covalent bonds
Be has the largest atomic radius in Group 2, allowing greater overlap with neighbouring atoms

metadata.title: Periodic trends: IE in Group 2, EA of the halogens
metadata.source: Example test #3 Q2
metadata.memoryHook: **IE falls down a group (the outer electron is further away and shielded) and rises across a period**: Be > Mg > Ca > Sr > Ba.

variants.stem: Which metal has the **largest** ionisation energy?
variants.explanation: IE decreases down the group as atoms grow (Be > Mg > Ca > Sr > Ba).

variants.explanation: Cl has the largest electron affinity; F is lower because of electron–electron repulsion in its compact 2p shell (F is still the most electronegative). (Example #X Q2.)

metadata.title: The inert-pair effect
metadata.source: Ch4 Group 13 slides; Ch4 Group 14 (Pb halides)
metadata.memoryHook: **The inert pair stays home**: poor d/f shielding holds the 6s² pair tight, so Tl prefers +1 and Pb prefers +2 over the group oxidation state.

variants.stem: Tl forms Tl₂O and stable Tl(I) halides, whereas Al forms Al₂O₃. Explain the inert-pair effect.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: From Period 4 on, filled d (and in Period 6 also 4f) shells are inserted before the p-block
d and f electrons shield poorly → 6s electrons feel a high effective nuclear charge and are held close to the nucleus
So the ns² pair is hard to remove/use in bonding → the +1 state (group oxidation state − 2) becomes more stable down the group (Tl⁺ > Tl³⁺; Pb²⁺ > Pb⁴⁺)

metadata.title: Lewis acidity of the boron trihalides
metadata.source: Example tests #2 Q7, #3 Q7 → past finals P1 Q2(b) (5 marks)

variants.stem: Within BF₃, BCl₃, BBr₃, which is the **weakest** Lewis acid?
variants.explanation: Order of Lewis acidity: BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃ (opposite to the electronegativity argument).

variants.stem: Explain why the Lewis acidity of BBr₃ is greater than that of BF₃.
variants.explanation: Electronegativity alone would predict BF₃ as the strongest acid — the observed order is set by X→B π bonding.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Lewis acidity comes from the empty B 2p_z orbital (LUMO) of trigonal planar BX₃
Filled p orbitals on X donate π density into B 2p_z (X→B π back-donation), partly filling it
π overlap is best for F (2p–2p, similar size and energy) and poorest for Br (4p–2p mismatch)
So BF₃ loses the most π stabilisation on pyramidalising to the sp³ adduct; BBr₃ loses least and binds bases more strongly

metadata.title: Why CO₂ is molecular but SiO₂ is a network
metadata.source: Tutorial 3 Q E; Ch4 Group 14 slides (silicon dioxide)
metadata.memoryHook: **C likes two double bonds; Si likes four single bonds.** So CO₂ is a small molecule (a gas) and SiO₂ is a giant 3D network (quartz, mp 1710 °C).

variants.stem: Bond energies (kcal mol⁻¹): C–O 86, C=O 193, Si–O 111, Si=O 153.
variants.explanation: 2 × 193 − 4 × 86 = 386 − 344 = 42 → carbon prefers two C=O (molecular CO₂ gas). 4 × 111 − 2 × 153 = 444 − 306 = 138 → silicon prefers four Si–O single bonds → 3D covalent network (quartz, mp 1710 °C).

metadata.title: Nitrogen reaction chart (Haber → nitric acid, hydrazine)
metadata.source: Example test #2 Q12 (6 marks)
metadata.memoryHook: **Ostwald (patents 1902, developed with Brauer; Kuhlmann had oxidised ammonia earlier) wanted nitric acid without Chilean saltpetre.** NH₃ burns over hot Pt with a very short contact time (longer contact lets NO decompose). **O‑S‑T**: **O**xidise NH₃ → NO, **S**econd oxidation → NO₂, **T**ake it up in water → HNO₃. Haber makes the NH₃.

variants.stem: N₂ + H₂ → **A** (Δ, Fe catalyst; Haber process). A + O₂ → **B** (Δ, Pt catalyst, −H₂O). B + O₂ → **C**. B + C → **D**. C + H₂O → **E** (+ B). (Scheme reconstructed from the Example #2 key.) A + NaOCl → **F** (−NaCl, −H₂O). A + E → NH₄NO₃. Identify A–F.
variants.explanation: Haber: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Catalytic oxidation (Pt, 1300 K): 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O. 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; NO + NO₂ → N₂O₃ (blue, only below −101 °C stable). 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO. Olin–Raschig: NH₃ + NaOCl → N₂H₄.

metadata.title: Haber–Bosch process
metadata.source: Ch4 Group 15 slides (N-hydrides, NH₃ in industry); Ch4 hydrogen reactivity slide
metadata.memoryHook: **Haber showed it in the lab (1909); Bosch and BASF made it industrial (1913), with Mittasch’s promoted iron catalyst.** N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ turns 4 gas molecules into 2, so **high pressure pushes the equilibrium right**; heat and the catalyst are for rate (the strong N≡N bond). The aim: fertiliser from air.

metadata.title: Phosphorus reaction scheme

metadata.memoryHook: **Phosphorus = “light-bearer”; Brand isolated it from urine around 1669.** White P₄ glows by chemiluminescence (slow oxidation in air), not stored light, and ignites in air. metadata.source: Ch4 Group 16 slides (sulfur hexafluoride)
metadata.memoryHook: **SF₆ is willing but kinetically inert**: thermodynamically favoured, yet unreactive under ordinary conditions. Only fluorine can take S to +6, directly: S + 3F₂ → SF₆.

variants.stem: SF₆ + 3H₂O → SO₃ + 6HF has ΔG° = −221 kJ mol⁻¹, yet SF₆ is the most inert covalent fluoride (used as a high-voltage insulating gas). Explain.
variants.explanation: Fluorine is the only halogen able to oxidise S to +6 (direct combination S + F₂ → SF₆).

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: The hydrolysis is thermodynamically favourable — the stability is kinetic, not thermodynamic
There is no low-energy pathway for attack: S has reached its maximum coordination number (6) and is shielded by six F atoms
Hence a very high activation energy / slow rate

metadata.title: Named processes → product
metadata.source: Ch4 slides (all named processes); Example tests #2 Q4, #3 Q9, #X Q5

variants.stem: Give the main (target) product of each named process.
variants.explanation: Haber N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃; Olin–Raschig 2NH₃ + NaOCl → N₂H₄; Wislicenus NaNH₂ + N₂O → NaN₃; contact SO₂ → SO₃ → oleum → H₂SO₄; water–gas shift CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂; chlor-alkali 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂.

variants.stem: In the past-test option lists, which of these is **not** a method for making a compound?
variants.explanation: The Grotthuss mechanism is proton hopping along hydrogen-bonded water wires (H₃O⁺ conduction) — it appears as a distractor.
variants.memoryHook: **Grotthuss = a proton relay, not a manufacturing process**: H⁺ hops along hydrogen-bonded water wires. It is named for Theodor von Grotthuss, whose electrolysis-of-water theory had charge passed along a chain of molecules.
variants.memoryHookNote: Sources date Grotthuss’s theory to about 1805–06, and none checked ties his original proposal precisely to the modern proton-relay mechanism.

metadata.title: Chirality from σ and Sₙ
metadata.source: Ch6 optical isomerism slides (σ, S_n; mirror plane and inversion centre) — drafted from course notes (unverified)

variants.stem: Which of these are **chiral**? Select all that apply.
variants.hint: Look for a mirror plane (σ = S₁) or inversion centre (i = S₂).
variants.explanation: [M(AA)₃] and cis-[M(AA)₂X₂] are propeller/skewed arrangements with no mirror plane or other improper axis, so they are chiral. trans-[CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ has a mirror plane (σ) and so is achiral; mer-[MA₃B₃] has a mirror plane containing the meridian; the square-planar complex lies in a σ_h plane (the molecular plane), so it is achiral.

variants.stem: A flat (planar) molecule such as square-planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] cannot be chiral because…
variants.explanation: Any molecule that lies in a mirror plane has σ (= S₁), so it is superimposable on its mirror image. A C_n axis alone does not rule out chirality (e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺ has C₃ and C₂ axes and is chiral).

options.label: its molecular plane is a mirror plane (σ_h), and σ = S₁ is an improper axis
planar molecules have no symmetry elements

variants.stem: A molecule is chiral if and only if it has no…

options.label: The metal site becomes more crowded, so an incoming ligand approaches less easily
With more ligands attached, the chance that one dissociates is higher (statistical factor)
Each added ligand increases the metal's positive charge
Later ligands are always weaker bases

variants.stem: For Cu²⁺(aq) + NH₃: log K₁ = 4.15, log K₂ = 3.50, log K₃ = 2.89, log K₄ = 2.13. What is log β₄?
variants.explanation: βₙ = K₁K₂…Kₙ, so log β₄ = Σ log Kᵢ = 12.67.

inputSlot.formatHint: 2 d.p.

metadata.title: The anomalous fifth formation constant of Cu(II)–NH₃
metadata.source: Tutorial 4 Q4(a); Ch7 Jahn–Teller slides (reactivity)

variants.stem: log K₁–K₄ for NH₃ binding to [Cu(OH₂)₆]²⁺ are 4.15, 3.50, 2.89, 2.13, but log K₅ = −0.52. Suggest why K₅ is so different.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: K₁ → K₄ fall steadily as expected on statistical grounds
K₅ drops sharply, signalling a change in coordination: a very stable square planar/tetragonal [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ forms
Cu²⁺ is d⁹: Jahn–Teller elongation leaves two long, weak axial bonds
So substitution beyond the fourth (equatorial) ammine is disfavoured → negative log K₅

metadata.title: Chelate and macrocyclic effects
metadata.source: Tutorial 4 Q4(b); Ch7 slides (chelate effect, Cd²⁺ data, macrocyclic effect)

variants.stem: [Cd(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4 CH₃NH₂: ΔH° = −57.3 kJ, ΔS° = −67.3 J K⁻¹; + 2 en: ΔH° = −56.5 kJ, ΔS° = +14.1 J K⁻¹. What drives the chelate effect here?
variants.explanation: ΔH° is nearly identical (both form four Cd–N bonds); −TΔS° is +20.1 vs −4.2 kJ mol⁻¹, giving ΔG° −37.2 vs −60.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (log β 6.52 vs 10.6).

options.label: Entropy: 2 en displace 4 H₂O, a net gain of two free molecules
Enthalpy: Cd–N bonds to en are much stronger
Both ΔH and ΔS favour CH₃NH₂
Steric strain in the methylamine complex

variants.stem: For Cu²⁺: log β₁(en) = 10.72 and log β₂(en) = 9.31 (stepwise), versus NH₃ log K₁ … K₄ = 4.15, 3.50, 2.89, 2.13. Compare and explain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Compare like with like: one en replaces two NH₃, so compare K(en,1) with K₁K₂(NH₃) (log 7.65) and K(en,2) with K₃K₄ (log 5.02)
en values are substantially larger → more favourable complex formation
Attributed to the chelate effect of the bidentate en ligand (mainly entropic)

variants.stem: Which statements are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: Macrocycles give even greater stability than open chelates: the ligand deformation needed to release a donor raises Eₐ for dissociation.

options.label: Kinetic chelate effect: after one end of a chelate dissociates, the dangling donor is held close and re-binds quickly
Macrocyclic effect: a preorganised ring loses no extra strain on binding but must deform strongly for a donor to dissociate
Macrocycles are less stable than the open-chain chelate analogues
The chelate effect arises because chelating ligands are always stronger σ-donors

metadata.title: Cu(II) affinity: NH₃ vs the halides
metadata.source: Ch7 practice Q1

variants.stem: Formation constants for one ligand substituting on aqueous Cu(II): order them.
variants.explanation: N in NH₃ is a better donor than F (less electronegative). Among halides, decreasing charge-to-radius ratio down the group (F⁻ highest) dominates over decreasing electronegativity, so F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻.

metadata.title: Stability order of metal ions and complexes
metadata.source: Ch7 practice Q2; Ch7 slides (questions on stability)

variants.stem: Order the M²⁺ ions by the stability of their complexes.
variants.explanation: Cu²⁺ > Ni²⁺ > Co²⁺ > Fe²⁺ > Mn²⁺ (course answer c): ionic radius decreases across the period, so charge-to-radius ratio is highest for Cu²⁺ and lowest for Mn²⁺. (This is the Irving–Williams order.)

variants.stem: Arrange in order of increasing stability: [Cr(en)₃]³⁺, [CrCl₆]³⁻, [CrF₆]³⁻, [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺.
variants.explanation: Cl⁻ (large, low charge density, poor base toward hard Cr³⁺) < F⁻ < NH₃ (better σ donor) < en (chelate effect).

variants.stem: Which favour a strong metal–ligand bond / stable complex? Select all.
variants.explanation: Bulky groups near the coordination site hinder approach and promote dissociation to relieve strain.

options.label: High charge-to-radius ratio of the metal ion
More basic ligand (higher charge-to-radius or dipole-to-size ratio)
Bulky groups near the donor atom

metadata.title: Valence bond theory: hybrids and its failure
metadata.source: Ch7 slides (valence bond theory)

variants.stem: Give the VBT hybridisation for each geometry.
variants.explanation: Inner-orbital octahedral complexes use (n−1)d (d²sp³); outer-orbital ones would use nd (sp³d²).

variants.stem: [CoF₆]³⁻ has four unpaired electrons, unlike almost all diamagnetic Co(III) complexes. Why does this expose a weakness of VBT?
variants.explanation: d²sp³ (using 3d) forces pairing → diamagnetic. Four unpaired electrons need the "outer" 4d set — energetically implausible. New concepts (CFT, LFT) are needed.

options.label: Explaining it needs sp³d² hybrids using 4d orbitals, which are far too high in energy to hybridise

metadata.title: Principles of crystal field theory
metadata.source: Past finals P3 Q3(b) (5 marks); Ch7 CFT slides

variants.stem: Describe the principles of crystal field theory and explain the origin of the splitting of the d orbitals in an octahedral complex.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Ligand lone pairs are modelled as point negative charges (purely electrostatic metal–ligand interaction)
These charges repel the metal d electrons, raising all d energies; in a spherical field the five d orbitals stay degenerate
In O_h, d_z² and d_x²−y² point directly at the ligands → stronger repulsion → raised (e_g)
d_xy, d_xz, d_yz point between the ligands → less repulsion → lowered (t₂g)
Splitting Δo; barycentre conserved: e_g +3/5 Δo, t₂g −2/5 Δo
Used to explain colour (d–d transitions), magnetism (high/low spin) and stability (CFSE)

metadata.title: Principles of ligand field theory
metadata.source: Past finals P3 Q3(c) (5 marks); Ch7 LFT slides

variants.stem: Describe the principles of ligand field theory and explain the origin of the splitting of the d orbitals in an octahedral complex.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: MO approach: metal valence orbitals combine with symmetry-adapted linear combinations (SALCs) of ligand orbitals
In O_h, metal orbitals sort by symmetry: 4s (a₁g), 4p (t₁u), d_z²/d_x²−y² (e_g), d_xy/d_xz/d_yz (t₂g); ligand σ SALCs are a₁g + t₁u + e_g
e_g d orbitals overlap with ligand SALCs → bonding (mainly ligand, hold the 12 ligand electrons) and antibonding e_g* (mainly metal)
t₂g has no σ SALC partner → nonbonding; Δo is the gap between t₂g and e_g*
π interactions shift t₂g: π-donors raise t₂g (smaller Δo), π-acceptors lower t₂g (larger Δo) — explaining the spectrochemical series

metadata.title: Limitations of crystal field theory
metadata.source: Past finals P3 Q3(d) (5 marks); Ch7 slide "Limitations of CFT"

variants.stem: What are the limitations of crystal field theory?

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Oversimplification: ligands treated as point charges/dipoles
Ignores covalency — no overlap between ligand and metal orbitals
Does not consider the type/nature of the ligand, so cannot explain the spectrochemical series (e.g. neutral CO is strong-field; anionic halides weak; OH⁻ below H₂O)
Ignores π bonding (π-donor / π-acceptor effects)
Cannot quantitatively match electronic spectra

metadata.title: Octahedral CFSE, unpaired electrons and pairing
metadata.source: Ch7 practice Q4; Ch7 slides (CFSE, high/low spin)

variants.stem: Octahedral CFSE (positive = stabilisation, as a coefficient of Δo), number of unpaired electrons, and number of extra pairing energies P relative to high spin.
variants.explanation: CFSE = 0.4 n(t₂g) − 0.6 n(e_g). d³ t₂g³ 1.2. HS d⁴ t₂g³e_g¹ 0.6. LS d⁴ t₂g⁴ 1.6 − P. LS d⁵ t₂g⁵ 2.0 − 2P, one unpaired. (HS d⁵ = 0.)

variants.stem: Same quantities for these octahedral configurations.
variants.explanation: HS d⁶ t₂g⁴e_g² 0.4 (4 unpaired). LS d⁶ t₂g⁶ 2.4 − 2P. LS d⁷ t₂g⁶e_g¹ 1.8 − P (1 unpaired). d⁸ t₂g⁶e_g² 1.2. d⁹ t₂g⁶e_g³ 0.6.

variants.stem: Tetrahedral CFSE = 0.6 n(e) − 0.4 n(t₂), in units of Δt (always high spin). Give the coefficient for each.
variants.explanation: d² e²: 1.2. d³ e²t₂¹: 1.2 − 0.4 = 0.8. d⁵ e²t₂³: 0. d⁷ e⁴t₂³: 2.4 − 1.2 = 1.2. d⁸ e⁴t₂⁴: 0.8.

metadata.title: When does spin state matter?
metadata.source: Ch7 practice Q4; Ch7 slides (high spin vs low spin)

variants.stem: For octahedral complexes, which dⁿ configurations can be either high spin or low spin? Select all.
variants.explanation: Only d⁴–d⁷ have a choice between occupying e_g and pairing in t₂g.

variants.stem: For d⁴, high spin (0.6 Δo) and low spin (1.6 Δo − P) compete. Low spin is preferred when…
variants.explanation: 1.6Δo − P > 0.6Δo ⟺ Δo > P. Pairing energy = coulomb repulsion in a doubly occupied orbital + loss of exchange energy.

variants.stem: Why are tetrahedral complexes almost always high spin?
variants.explanation: Only 4 ligands, and none points directly at a d orbital.

options.label: Δt ≈ 4/9 Δo is small, below the pairing energy
Tetrahedral complexes have no t₂ set

metadata.title: Spectrochemical series and metal dependence of Δo
metadata.source: Ch7 slides (factors affecting Δ); Ch7 practice Q5

variants.stem: Order the ligands by field strength (spectrochemical series).
variants.explanation: I⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO: π-donors at the weak end, σ-only donors in the middle, π-acceptors at the strong end.

variants.stem: Order by Δo.
variants.explanation: Higher charge → shorter, stronger M–L interaction → larger Δo (Fe²⁺ < Fe³⁺). Down a group 4d/5d orbitals are larger and interact more strongly (Co < Rh < Ir). NH₃ > H₂O also raises the Co(III) values.

metadata.title: Δo for Cr(III) complexes from σ/π properties
metadata.source: Ch7 practice Q5

variants.stem: For Cr(III), Δo increases Cl⁻ < F⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ ≈ en < CN⁻. Explain in terms of σ and π donor/acceptor properties.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Cl⁻ is a fairly good π-donor → raises t₂g → smallest Δo
F⁻ is a weaker π-donor than Cl⁻ (next)
H₂O is a very weak π-donor (only one lone pair not used in σ bonding)
NH₃ and en are σ-only: no lone pairs or suitable orbitals for π
CN⁻ is a good π-acceptor (empty π*) → lowers t₂g → largest Δo

metadata.title: σ-only, π-donor or π-acceptor?
metadata.source: Ch7 LFT slides (π-bonding, ligand types)

variants.stem: Classify each ligand as **σ-only**, **π-donor** or **π-acceptor**.
variants.explanation: π-donors (dπ–pπ): halides, OH⁻, O²⁻, RO⁻, H₂O. π-acceptors (dπ–π* or dπ–dπ/σ*): CO, CN⁻, PR₃, pyridine, NO₂⁻, ethylene. σ-only: NH₃, en, H⁻, CH₃⁻.

metadata.title: How π bonding changes Δo
metadata.source: Ch7 LFT slides (L→M π bonding, M→L back bonding); Tutorial 4 Q5

variants.stem: Which statements are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: M→L back-bonding needs an electron-rich, low-oxidation-state metal; high oxidation states already lack electrons.

options.label: π-donor ligands: filled ligand π orbitals lie below t₂g; t₂g becomes antibonding (t₂g*), raised → Δo decreases
π-acceptor ligands: empty ligand π* lie above t₂g; t₂g becomes bonding, lowered → Δo increases
Back-bonding is most favourable for metals in high oxidation states
In a σ-only complex the t₂g set is nonbonding

variants.stem: H⁻ and PPh₃ are both strong-field ligands, but only PPh₃ is a π-acceptor. Is π-acceptor character required for strong-field behaviour? What orbital factors make each ligand strong?

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: No: H⁻ has no low-energy π-symmetry acceptor orbitals yet is very strong-field
Very strong σ-bases (H⁻, CH₃⁻) push the e_g* level up strongly → large Δo
π-acceptors (PPh₃, CO) instead lower t₂g by back-bonding → large Δo; two routes to a large splitting

metadata.title: Effect of back-bonding on the C–O bond
metadata.source: Ch7 practice Q6; Ch7 slides (question: C≡O stronger or weaker)

variants.stem: When CO binds an electron-rich metal centre, the C–O bond…
variants.explanation: M→CO π back-donation populates CO π* (antibonding), lowering the C–O bond order: longer C–O, lower ν(CO), stronger M–C.

options.label: lengthens and weakens, because metal d electrons enter the CO π* orbitals
shortens, because σ donation removes antibonding density

metadata.title: Tetrahedral vs octahedral splitting
metadata.source: Ch7 CFT slides (tetrahedral field)

variants.stem: Which statements about tetrahedral splitting are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: In T_d the t₂ orbitals point toward the cube edges (closer to ligands) and e toward the faces; no orbital points directly at a ligand.

options.label: The lower set is e (d_z², d_x²−y²) and the upper set t₂ (d_xy, d_xz, d_yz)
Labels carry no g/u because T_d has no inversion centre
e is stabilised by 3/5 Δt and t₂ destabilised by 2/5 Δt
d_xy, d_xz, d_yz point at the ligands in T_d

metadata.title: Tetragonal distortion to square planar
metadata.source: Ch7 practice Q7; Ch7 slides (square planar system)

variants.stem: Order the d orbitals for a square planar complex (ligands on ±x, ±y).
variants.explanation: Removing the z-ligands stabilises every orbital with z character (d_z², d_xz, d_yz) and destabilises d_xy, d_x²−y². d_x²−y² stays far above the rest.

variants.stem: Which statements are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: Elongation along z reduces repulsion for z-type orbitals (stabilised), raising d_xy and d_x²−y² by compensating amounts.

options.label: d⁸ with strong-field ligands favours square planar geometry (e.g. [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, [PdCl₄]²⁻, [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺)
Square planar d⁸ complexes are low spin with the d_x²−y² orbital empty
On tetragonal elongation, d_z², d_xz, d_yz are destabilised

metadata.title: Why tetrahedral Co(II) is common but tetrahedral Ni(II) is not
metadata.source: Ch7 slides (question: Co(II) vs Ni(II) tetrahedral complexes)

variants.stem: Assume Δt = 4/9 Δo and high spin throughout. Give each CFSE as a coefficient of **Δo**.
variants.explanation: Co²⁺: oct t₂g⁵e_g² 0.8 Δo; tet e⁴t₂³ 1.2 Δt = 0.53 Δo → loses only 0.27 Δo on going tetrahedral. Ni²⁺: oct t₂g⁶e_g² 1.2 Δo; tet e⁴t₂⁴ 0.8 Δt = 0.36 Δo → loses 0.84 Δo. Ni(II) has a much larger octahedral preference, so its tetrahedral complexes are rarer/less stable.

metadata.title: Electron bookkeeping in the octahedral MO diagram
metadata.source: Ch7 LFT slides (MO diagrams of [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and [CoF₆]³⁻)

variants.stem: σ-only MO diagram of octahedral [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ (large Δo) and [CoF₆]³⁻ (small Δo):
variants.explanation: Six ligand lone pairs fill the six bonding MOs (mostly ligand character). The six Co³⁺ d electrons go into t₂g (nonbonding) and e_g* (antibonding): t₂g⁶ for NH₃ (low spin, diamagnetic); t₂g⁴e_g*² for F⁻ (high spin, 4 unpaired).

fields.label: Number of σ-bonding MOs (a₁g + t₁u + e_g)

metadata.title: Jahn–Teller distortions and their consequences
metadata.source: Ch7 Jahn–Teller slides; Tutorial 4 Q6

variants.stem: Which statements are correct? Select all.
variants.explanation: JT is too weak in T_d (no d orbital points at the ligands); the size and sense of distortion cannot be predicted. t₂g asymmetry gives only weak distortions.

options.label: A complex with degenerate, asymmetrically filled orbitals distorts to remove the degeneracy
Distortion is strong for e_g¹ or e_g³ (high-spin d⁴, low-spin d⁷, d⁹) because e_g* is σ-antibonding
Axial elongation is more common than compression (it weakens two bonds rather than four)
The Jahn–Teller effect is large in tetrahedral complexes
Its magnitude and direction can be predicted exactly from dⁿ

variants.stem: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) should show one d–d band, but a band with a shoulder (two close components) is seen. Why?
variants.explanation: The excited configuration (e_g¹) is Jahn–Teller active; the small splitting gives a shoulder rather than a separate band.

options.label: Jahn–Teller distortion splits e_g (and t₂g), giving two close transitions

variants.stem: Account for the observation that two separate water-exchange rates are found for [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Cu²⁺ is d⁹ (t₂g⁶e_g³): degenerate e_g asymmetrically filled → Jahn–Teller distortion
Tetragonal elongation creates two kinds of water: axial (long Cu–O) and equatorial (short)
Different bond lengths/strengths → different exchange rates (axial waters exchange faster)

metadata.title: Using μ to infer spin state
metadata.source: Ch8 slides (questions on magnetism; Gouy balance)

metadata.title: d–d absorption of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ and complementary colour
metadata.source: Ch8 slides (question: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ at 20,300 cm⁻¹; complementary colours)

variants.stem: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ shows one band with maximum at 20,300 cm⁻¹.

metadata.title: Substitution mechanisms and rate laws
metadata.source: Ch9 slides (D, A, I mechanisms; steady-state rate laws)

variants.stem: Name the mechanism (D, A or I).
variants.explanation: D is analogous to S_N1 (CN decreases); A increases CN; I has no detectable intermediate. A vs I is decided by whether an intermediate can be detected (or a stereochemical change shows it lived long enough to rearrange).

fields.label: Leaving ligand departs first to give a lower-CN intermediate
Entering ligand binds first to give a higher-CN intermediate
Concerted bond making/breaking through a single transition state, no intermediate

variants.stem: For ML₅X + Y → ML₅Y + X, which rate laws apply in the limits given? Select all.
variants.explanation: Steady state for the D intermediate ML₅: rate = k₁k₂[ML₅X][Y]/(k₋₁[X] + k₂[Y]) → k₁[ML₅X] when k₂[Y] dominates. For A: rate = k₁k₂[ML₅X][Y]/(k₋₁ + k₂) → k₁[ML₅X][Y].

options.label: D, with k₂[Y] ≫ k₋₁[X]: rate = k₁[ML₅X]
A, with k₂ ≫ k₋₁: rate = k₁[ML₅X][Y]

variants.stem: Substitution on [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ shows large rate variations as the incoming ligand changes. This points to…

variants.explanation: Kinetic chelate effect: the intermediate concentration is low and the first dissociation easily reverses.

Chelate M–L bonds are covalent; monodentate bonds are ionic
Chelates react only by an associative mechanism

Via a trigonal-bipyramidal intermediate: mixtures form, with cis products predominating

metadata.title: Trans-effect series
metadata.source: Ch9 slides (trans effect)

variants.stem: Order the ligands by trans effect (kinetic, transition-state series).
variants.explanation: C₂H₄ ≈ CO > CN⁻ > NO₂⁻ > SCN⁻ > I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > NH₃. π-acceptors stabilise the 5-coordinate transition state.

π effect: a π-acceptor T withdraws metal density in the 5-coordinate transition state, stabilising it
Trans influence is a ground-state (thermodynamic) effect; the π contribution is a transition-state (kinetic) effect
The trans effect is seen only in octahedral complexes
