metadata.title: Counting σ and π bonds in the valence-bond picture
metadata.source: Ch1 Valence Bond Theory slides (σ/π overlap; ethylene, acetylene) — drafted from course notes (unverified)

variants.stem: Give the number of σ bonds and π bonds in each molecule: ethene (C₂H₄), ethyne (C₂H₂) and N₂.
variants.hint: A single bond is one σ; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π.
variants.explanation: Every bond contains exactly one σ bond; each additional bond in a double or triple bond is a π bond. C₂H₄: 4 C–H + 1 C–C σ = 5 σ, 1 π. C₂H₂: 2 C–H + 1 C–C = 3 σ, 2 π. N≡N: 1 σ, 2 π.

variants.stem: In valence bond theory, which statement about σ and π bonds is correct?
variants.explanation: A σ bond has cylindrical symmetry about the bond axis and is formed by end-to-end overlap, which is normally the largest overlap and so the strongest. A π bond is formed by side-by-side overlap of p orbitals, with a nodal plane containing the axis. A π bond always accompanies a σ bond in the course treatment.

options.label: σ: end-to-end (head-on) overlap along the bond axis; π: side-by-side overlap with electron density above and below the axis
σ: side-by-side overlap; π: end-to-end overlap along the bond axis
π bonds are stronger than σ bonds because side-by-side overlap is always greater
A π bond can exist between two atoms without a σ bond

metadata.title: Formal charges and resonance forms of thiocyanate, SCN⁻
metadata.source: Ch1 Formal Charge slide (SCN⁻ with S–C / C–N bond-length table) — drafted from course notes (unverified)

variants.stem: Structure A of SCN⁻ is S=C=N with two lone pairs on S and two lone pairs on N. Give the formal charge on each atom of A.
variants.hint: Formal charge = (valence e⁻) − (non-bonding e⁻) − (number of bonds).
variants.explanation: Formal charge = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − number of bonds. S: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. C: 4 − 0 − 4 = 0. N: 5 − 4 − 2 = −1. The sum is −1, the charge of the ion.

variants.stem: Three Lewis structures of SCN⁻ are drawn: A: S=C=N (negative charge on N); B: S–C≡N (negative charge on S); C: S≡C–N with S carrying one lone pair and N three. Which contributes least?
variants.explanation: In C the formal charges are S +1, C 0, N −2: charge is separated and the −2 sits on N while the more electropositive S is positive. A (N −1) and B (S −1) each have a single −1 formal charge, so C is the least favourable.

variants.stem: In NaSCN the S–C distance is 165 pm and the C–N distance is 118 pm. Reference lengths: S–C single 181, double 155 pm; C–N double 128, triple 116 pm. What do these lengths indicate?
variants.explanation: Neither bond matches a pure single, double or triple reference length: S–C (165 pm) lies between 181 and 155 pm, and C–N (118 pm) lies between 128 and 116 pm, close to the triple bond. The real ion is therefore a hybrid of A and B, with C contributing little.

options.label: SCN⁻ is a resonance hybrid of A and B: S–C is between single and double, C–N is between double and triple
SCN⁻ is purely structure A, with a C–N double bond
SCN⁻ is purely structure B, with a C–S single bond
SCN⁻ is mainly structure C, with a C≡S triple bond

metadata.title: Which element E gives the expanded-octet anion [EO₄]⁻?
metadata.source: Tutorial 1 (RK1) Q D — drafted from course notes (unverified)

variants.stem: A Lewis structure shows E at the centre of four O atoms with an overall charge of −1, i.e. [EO₄]⁻. Select the possible E from H, S, He, P, Xe, Br, B, Si.
variants.hint: Count the total valence electrons of [EO₄]⁻ and see how many E must contribute.
variants.explanation: Valence electrons: 4 O × 6 + 1 (charge) = 25, so E must supply 32 − 25 = 7: a halogen, Br. Br can also exceed an octet (period 4), which the structure requires. S would give SO₄²⁻, P PO₄³⁻, Si SiO₄⁴⁻ and Xe neutral XeO₄; H and He cannot form four bonds.

variants.stem: Explain why E must be Br and not S, P, Si or Xe.
variants.explanation: See the working in the previous part. The −1 charge fixes E as a 7-electron element; the other period-3 or heavier candidates would require different overall charges.

metadata.title: First and successive ionisation energies
metadata.source: Ch2 Ionic Bonding slide (IE and EA definitions); Ch1 IE-vs-Z plot; Group 1 and 2 property tables — drafted from course notes (unverified)
metadata.memoryHook: **IE falls down a group and rises across a period**, so a Group 2 atom is higher than its Group 1 neighbour (Na < Li, Mg < Be).

variants.stem: Rank the first ionisation energies of Li (123), Na (118.5), Be (215) and Mg (176 kcal/mol) from highest to lowest.
variants.explanation: Going down a group IE falls (Na < Li, Mg < Be) because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded. Going across a period IE rises, so Group 2 elements are higher than their Group 1 neighbours: Be > Mg > Li > Na (215 > 176 > 123 > 118.5).

variants.stem: The third ionisation energy of Mg is far larger than its second. Why?
variants.explanation: Successive IEs rise because the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons. A very large jump occurs when removal starts from a shell nearer the nucleus (less shielding), which is why Mg forms Mg²⁺ and not Mg³⁺.

options.label: The third electron is removed from the filled inner shell, which is closer to the nucleus and much less shielded
The third electron is removed from a 3s orbital
Mg²⁺ has a lower nuclear charge than Mg⁺

metadata.title: Classifying orbital overlaps: σ, π or none
metadata.source: Textbook ch. 5.1 (MO from s and p orbitals), course Ch3 — drafted from course notes (unverified)

variants.stem: Take the z axis as the line joining the two nuclei. Classify the overlap of each pair of orbitals.
variants.hint: Answer σ, π or none.
variants.explanation: σ orbitals are symmetric to rotation about the internuclear axis: s–s and pz–pz (head-on). π orbitals come from px–px or py–py (side-by-side) and change sign on C₂ rotation. px with pz has equal positive and negative overlap, so the net overlap is zero and no MO forms.

variants.stem: Which pair of orbitals has zero net overlap and so does not combine to form a bonding/antibonding MO pair?
variants.explanation: The overlap region between 2px and 2pz has equal positive and negative contributions that cancel. The other pairs have symmetry-allowed overlap (s–pz and pz–pz give σ; px–px gives π).

options.label: 2s on A with 2pz on B (z = bond axis)

variants.explanation: π donors (Cl⁻) lower Δo, ligands with no π effect (NH₃) give intermediate Δo, and π acceptors (CO) raise Δo: Cl⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < CO.

variants.stem: Using CFSE = [n(t₂g) × ⅖Δo] − [n(eg) × ⅗Δo] (stabilisation positive), calculate the CFSE of d¹, d² and d³ in an octahedral field. Enter the coefficient of Δo.

variants.stem: Determine the CFSE (coefficient of Δo) for: high-spin d⁵, high-spin d⁶, low-spin d⁶, d⁹. For low-spin d⁶ also give the number of extra electron pairs that cost pairing energy P.
variants.explanation: HS d⁵ (t₂g³eg²): 1.2 − 1.2 = 0. HS d⁶ (t₂g⁴eg²): 1.6 − 1.2 = 0.4Δo. LS d⁶ (t₂g⁶): 2.4Δo − 2P (two more pairs than the high-spin configuration). d⁹ (t₂g⁶eg³): 2.4 − 1.8 = 0.6Δo.

variants.stem: Compare the geometry at nitrogen in N(SiH₃)₃ and N(CH₃)₃.
variants.explanation: N(CH₃)₃ is pyramidal (C–N–C about 108°), like NH₃. N(SiH₃)₃ is unusual: nitrogen is trigonal planar (N–Si 1.74 Å).

options.label: N(SiH₃)₃ is trigonal planar at N; N(CH₃)₃ is pyramidal

variants.stem: Explain the planar structure of N(SiH₃)₃. Give the traditional p,d-π explanation and say how the notes qualify it.
variants.explanation: The classical rationalisation is p,d-π overlap between the N lone pair and Si 3d orbitals, which would give Si–N partial double-bond character and a planar N. The notes call this a convenient but largely untrue explanation: weak electronic interactions are responsible, and the pyramidal–planar energy difference at nitrogen is very small.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: The nitrogen of N(SiH₃)₃ is trigonal planar (N–Si 1.74 Å), unlike pyramidal NH₃ and N(CH₃)₃ (C–N–C ≈ 108°); the N lone pair sits in a p orbital perpendicular to the plane
Traditional explanation: p,d-π bonding — the N lone pair overlaps side-by-side with an empty Si 3d orbital, giving partial Si–N double-bond character and a planar N
Weakness stated in the notes: there seems to be little truth to the p,d-π explanation (Si 3d orbitals are not significantly involved); it is only a convenient, easy model

The planarity is better attributed to weak electronic interactions (e.g. negative hyperconjugation into σ*(Si–H)); the energy difference between pyramidal and planar N is very small (about 5.9 kcal/mol even for NH₃)

metadata.title: Ostwald process (nitric acid from ammonia)
metadata.source: Added at the student's request; steps from the Ch4 nitrogen reaction chart
metadata.memoryHook: **Ostwald (patents 1902, developed with Brauer; Kuhlmann had oxidised ammonia earlier) wanted nitric acid without Chilean saltpetre.** NH₃ burns over hot Pt with a very short contact time (longer contact lets NO decompose). **O‑S‑T**: **O**xidise NH₃ → NO, **S**econd oxidation → NO₂, **T**ake it up in water → HNO₃. Haber makes the NH₃.

variants.stem: Name the industrial process that converts ammonia into nitric acid, via NO and NO₂ over a platinum catalyst.
variants.explanation: The **Ostwald process**: NH₃ is oxidised to NO over Pt, NO is oxidised to NO₂, and NO₂ is absorbed in water to give HNO₃.

inputSlot.formatHint: Name of the process

variants.stem: Write the equations for the Ostwald process from NH₃ to HNO₃ (Pt catalyst, about 1300 K for the first step).
variants.explanation: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt, 1300 K); 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO (the NO is recycled). Overall NH₃ + 2O₂ → HNO₃ + H₂O.

metadata.title: Downs cell (sodium from molten NaCl)
metadata.source: Added at the student's request; Ch4 Group 1 (fused-salt electrolysis)
metadata.memoryHook: **J. Cloyd Downs patented the cell in 1924**: electrolyse molten NaCl directly, with CaCl₂ added to lower the melting temperature, instead of making Na from NaOH (Davy 1807, then Castner). Na forms at the cathode, Cl₂ at the anode. In water, H₂O is reduced first, so you get NaOH.

variants.stem: Sodium metal is made industrially by electrolysing molten NaCl. Name the cell or process.
variants.explanation: The **Downs cell**: Na⁺ is reduced to liquid Na at the cathode and Cl⁻ is oxidised to Cl₂ at the anode (2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂).

inputSlot.formatHint: Name of the cell or process

variants.stem: Explain why sodium metal cannot be made by electrolysing aqueous NaCl, and what is made at the cathode instead.
variants.explanation: In water, H₂O is reduced in preference to Na⁺ (Na⁺/Na is far more negative), so H₂ and OH⁻ form. Molten NaCl has no water, so Na⁺ is reduced to Na.

variants.stem:
The diagram is the Tanabe–Sugano diagram of a d⁴ octahedral complex. The dashed line marks Δo/B = 12.

On a Tanabe–Sugano diagram the **ground state is always the horizontal axis** (E/B = 0): every other level is drawn above it. Find the label of the line that lies along the axis at the dashed line.
variants.hint: Go up the dashed line to the bottom of the diagram. The line that runs along the axis there is the ground state; read its label at the right-hand edge. The number of unpaired electrons is the spin multiplicity minus 1 (a quintet has 4).
variants.explanation: At Δo/B = 12 the line along the axis is ⁵Eg. Its spin multiplicity is 5, so there are 4 unpaired electrons, which is the high-spin arrangement for d⁴ (the diagram's vertical kink is the spin crossover; the ground state changes there).

metadata.title: Tanabe–Sugano 2: the spin-allowed bands, in order
metadata.source: Guided Tanabe–Sugano practice (diagram computed in-app)

variants.stem:
The diagram is the Tanabe–Sugano diagram of a d³ octahedral complex, and the dashed line marks Δo/B = 12.

A transition is **spin-allowed** only if the excited state has the same spin multiplicity as the ground state. First find the ground state at the dashed line; then, among the labelled lines of that same multiplicity, name the ones above it in order of increasing height at the dashed line (use the ruler). Give each as a term symbol.
variants.hint: Read the multiplicity (the small number in front of the letter) of the ground state. Ignore every line with a different number. Order the rest by their height above the axis where the dashed line crosses them.
variants.explanation: The ground state at Δo/B = 12 is ⁴A₂g, multiplicity 4. The lines with multiplicity 4 above it, from the lowest up, are ⁴T₂g (E/B ≈ 12.0), ⁴T₁g (E/B ≈ 19.3), ⁴T₁g (E/B ≈ 31.7): 3 spin-allowed bands. Lines of any other multiplicity give spin-forbidden bands, which are weak.

metadata.title: Tanabe–Sugano 5: the spin crossover
metadata.source: Guided Tanabe–Sugano practice (diagram computed in-app)

variants.stem:
The diagram is the Tanabe–Sugano diagram of a d⁴ octahedral complex. Somewhere along the horizontal axis the ground state changes: the line along the axis bends and a different line takes its place.

Give the Δo/B at which this spin crossover happens, the ground state before it (weak field) and after it (strong field), and the number of unpaired electrons on each side.
variants.hint: Follow the horizontal axis from the left: the first label is the weak-field (high-spin) ground state. The place where the axis line is replaced by another line is the crossover; the new label is the strong-field (low-spin) ground state. Unpaired electrons = multiplicity − 1.
variants.explanation: Weak field (left of Δo/B ≈ 27.3): ⁵Eg, 4 unpaired electrons (high spin). Strong field (right): ³T₁g, 2 unpaired (low spin). The crossover is where the pairing energy P equals the cost of putting an electron in e_g, so it marks the switch from high to low spin.

metadata.title: Tanabe–Sugano 6: explain the method
metadata.source: Guided Tanabe–Sugano practice (diagram computed in-app)

variants.stem: Explain how to use a Tanabe–Sugano diagram to get Δo and B for a d⁷ complex from two measured absorption bands. State what the axes mean, which bands to use, and what you do with the ratio.
variants.explanation: Both axes are scaled by B: the horizontal axis is Δo/B and the vertical axis is E/B, measured from the ground state (the horizontal axis itself). Only spin-allowed transitions are used: those to states with the same multiplicity as the ground state. Measure the energies of two such bands; their ratio is independent of B, so find the Δo/B at which the heights of the two corresponding lines have that ratio. variants.perspectiveLabel: d³ degeneracies and the repeated ²D
variants.stem: The d³ configuration (120 microstates) gives the terms 4F, 4P, 2H, 2G, 2F, 2D and 2P, with one of them occurring more than once. Give the number of microstates (2L+1)(2S+1) in each of ⁴F, ⁴P, ²H and ²G, and say how many times ²D occurs so that the microstates add up to 120.
variants.hint: (2L+1)(2S+1) for each term; the terms must add to 120. Whatever is missing after the other six terms is made up by the repeated term.
variants.explanation: ⁴F = 7×4 = 28, ⁴P = 3×4 = 12, ²H = 11×2 = 22, ²G = 9×2 = 18, ²F = 7×2 = 14, ²P = 3×2 = 6, and each ²D = 5×2 = 10. 100 microstates are in the six non-²D terms, so 120 − 100 = 20 = 2 × 10: ²D occurs 2 times.

metadata.title: Draw it: d-orbital splitting with the electrons and the CFSE
metadata.source: Template of 2025-26 Q3(a) (splitting diagram and CFSE of a given complex); draw on paper, then tick the marking points

variants.stem: Draw the d-orbital splitting diagram for the metal in KMnO₄ (assume tetrahedral or octahedral, as appropriate). Label the orbital sets, show the electrons and give the CFSE.
variants.explanation: Mn(VII) is d⁰. Four donors give a tetrahedron: e below t₂ with gap Δt (about 4/9 Δo). With no d electrons there is nothing to stabilise, CFSE = 0. (The purple colour is a ligand-to-metal charge transfer, not a d–d band.)

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Oxidation state Mn(VII), so d⁰; four oxide donors, so tetrahedral
Two sets drawn with the gap labelled Δt: e (d_z², d_x²−y²) lower and t₂ (d_xy, d_xz, d_yz) upper
e BELOW t₂ (the inverse of octahedral), centred on the free-ion level
No d electrons shown; CFSE = 0

variants.stem: Draw the d-orbital splitting diagram for K[Cr(H₂O)₂(C₂O₄)₂]·3H₂O. Label the orbital sets, show the electrons and give the CFSE.
variants.explanation: d³ in an octahedron: t₂g³ e_g⁰, three unpaired electrons, CFSE = −1.2 Δo. Weak or strong field makes no difference for d³.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Cr(III), d³, six donors (two H₂O and two bidentate oxalates), so octahedral
t₂g (d_xy, d_xz, d_yz) LOWER by 0.4 Δo and e_g (d_z², d_x²−y²) UPPER by 0.6 Δo, gap Δo labelled
Three electrons in three separate t₂g orbitals, parallel spins (Hund); e_g empty
CFSE = 3 × (−0.4 Δo) = −1.2 Δo (no pairing either way)

variants.stem: Draw the d-orbital splitting diagram for the metal in [Ni(NH₃)Cl(NH₂CH₃)₂]Cl (assume tetrahedral or octahedral, as appropriate). Label the orbital sets, show the electrons and give the CFSE.
variants.explanation: Four donors means a tetrahedron when the question says to choose between tetrahedral and octahedral. Fill e then t₂: e⁴ t₂⁴ puts two electrons singly in t₂ (paramagnetic). CFSE = −0.8 Δt.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Ni(II), d⁸; four donors (NH₃, Cl⁻ and two NH₂CH₃), so tetrahedral
e (lower, −0.6 Δt) and t₂ (upper, +0.4 Δt) drawn and labelled with the gap Δt
Eight electrons: e⁴ t₂⁴, with the last two electrons in separate t₂ orbitals (two unpaired)

variants.stem: Draw the splitting diagrams for [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ side by side. Show the electrons, say which is high spin and which low spin, and give each CFSE.
variants.explanation: Same metal ion and d count; only the ligands change Δo. Weak field: spread the electrons (Δo < P). Strong field: pair first (Δo > P). The low-spin d⁶ ion has two more pairs than the high-spin one, hence the 2P.

rubric.criterion: Both Fe(II), d⁶, octahedral; the ligand sets the size of Δo (H₂O weak, CN⁻ strong)
H₂O: Δo smaller than the pairing energy P, so t₂g⁴ e_g² (four unpaired, high spin); CFSE = 4(−0.4) + 2(+0.6) = −0.4 Δo
CN⁻: Δo larger than P, so t₂g⁶ (no unpaired, low spin, diamagnetic); CFSE = −2.4 Δo + 2P
States the rule: electrons pair before occupying e_g only when Δo > P

variants.stem: Draw the d-orbital splitting for square-planar [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ and fill in the electrons. Why is it diamagnetic?
variants.explanation: The ligands lie on x and y, so d_x²−y² is far above the rest. Eight electrons pair in d_xz, d_yz, d_z² and d_xy, which is why d⁸ strong-field complexes are square planar and diamagnetic.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Ni(II) d⁸ with four strong-field CN⁻ donors in the xy plane, so square planar (a tetragonal distortion of octahedral with the axial ligands removed)
Order from the top: d_x²−y² (points at the ligands) ≫ d_xy > d_z² > d_xz, d_yz (lowest, degenerate pair)
Eight electrons fill the four lower orbitals in pairs; d_x²−y² empty
No unpaired electrons: diamagnetic, because the large gap above the fourth orbital outweighs the pairing energy

variants.stem: Draw the d-orbital splitting of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ including the tetragonal (Jahn–Teller) distortion. Show the electrons and say why the distortion lowers the energy.
variants.explanation: An uneven e_g occupation (d⁹, and high-spin d⁴) is removed by distorting the octahedron. The d_z² pair is lowered and the single d_x²−y² electron raised, so there is a net energy gain.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Cu(II), d⁹: t₂g⁶ e_g³, an unevenly filled e_g set
Elongation along z: d_z² drops and d_x²−y² rises (e_g splits); d_xz, d_yz drop and d_xy rises (t₂g splits)
Electrons: (d_xz,d_yz)⁴ (d_xy)² (d_z²)² (d_x²−y²)¹, one unpaired
Net stabilisation comes from e_g (two electrons lowered by δ/2, one raised by δ/2); the filled t₂g set gives none

variants.stem: Draw the valence MO diagrams of N₂ and O₂ (include the effect of s–p mixing where it applies). Give each bond order and say whether it is paramagnetic.
variants.explanation: s–p mixing pushes σ2p up when the 2s–2p gap is small (up to N₂); from O₂ on, the gap is large and σ2p lies below π2p. Bond order = (bonding − antibonding)/2.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Atomic 2s and 2p columns each side with the eight MOs between them: σ2s, σ*2s, π2p, σ2p, π*2p, σ*2p
N₂ (s–p mixing): π2p BELOW σ2p; 10 valence electrons give bond order 3, diamagnetic
O₂ (no mixing): σ2p BELOW π2p; 12 valence electrons fill up to π*2p
O₂: two unpaired electrons in the degenerate π*2p pair (parallel), bond order 2, paramagnetic

variants.stem: Draw the valence MO diagram of CO. Show which orbitals are the HOMO and LUMO and where they sit, and give the bond order.
variants.explanation: Because the HOMO is mostly a carbon lone pair, CO binds through C. The empty π* orbitals accept electron density back from the metal, which strengthens M–C and weakens C–O.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Atomic orbitals offset: O lower than C (more electronegative)
Ten valence electrons fill σ(2s), σ*(2s), the two π bonds and the σ(2p); bond order 3
HOMO is the σ orbital, mainly on carbon (the carbon lone pair)
LUMO is the degenerate π* pair, mainly on carbon
Binding to a metal: σ donation from the C lone pair, π back-donation into π*

variants.stem: Draw the σ-only MO diagram of an octahedral complex ML₆. Label the metal and ligand-group orbitals by symmetry and show where Δo appears.
variants.explanation: Only e_g (d_z², d_x²−y²) points at the ligands, so only e_g can mix with the ligand a₁g/t₁u/e_g group orbitals; t₂g stays non-bonding. The t₂g–e_g* gap is Δo, which is why CFT and LFT give the same splitting pattern.

inputSlot.placeholder: Write the key points (or tick the box if you answered on paper)…

rubric.criterion: Metal orbitals: 4s (a₁g), 4p (t₁u), 3d split into e_g and t₂g
Six ligand group orbitals (σ): a₁g + t₁u + e_g
Bonding MOs a₁g, t₁u, e_g (mostly ligand, twelve ligand electrons); antibonding a₁g*, t₁u*, e_g*
t₂g non-bonding (metal d only), with the metal d electrons going into t₂g and e_g*
Δo = the gap between t₂g and e_g*

variants.stem: Draw the valence MO diagram of H₂O (bent, C₂v) and show its electrons.
variants.explanation: The H 1s group orbitals have a₁ and b₂ symmetry; the O 2p_x (out of plane) has b₁ symmetry and no partner, so it stays non-bonding. That is the second lone pair seen in photoelectron spectra.

rubric.criterion: O 2s, 2p and the two H 1s group orbitals (a₁ and b₂) combine
Bonding MOs: 1a₁ (mostly O 2s), 1b₂, 2a₁; antibonding 3a₁* and 2b₂*
1b₁ is a non-bonding pure O 2p orbital (out of the molecular plane): the HOMO
Eight valence electrons fill 1a₁, 1b₂, 2a₁, 1b₁
